pat301.t: Fusarium Wilt - Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici
s: Fusarium Wilt - Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici
Symptoms: The first symptom of the disease yellowing of the lower leaves and affected leaflets wilt and die.The symptoms continue in subsequent leaves.
Mode of spread and survival: The fungus is seed-borne and soil-borne.
Wind-borne macro-conidia and micro-conidia help in distribution of the pathogen from field to field.
Management: The affected plants should be removed and destroyed.

pat301.t: Early blight - Alternaria tomatophila (syn: Alternaria solani)
s: Early blight - Alternaria tomatophila (syn: Alternaria solani)
Symptoms: Disease symptoms observed as small, black lesions mostly on the older foliage.
Lesions on the stems are similar to those on leaves, sometimes girdling the plant if they occur near the soil line.
Pathogen: Mycelium is septate, branched and light brown colour.
Conidia are beaked, muriform, dark coloured and borne singly.
Late blight: Phyotophthora infestans
Symptoms Water soaked brown to purplish lessions with faded green patches appears in leaves, spread fast to entire leaf and petiole.
In leaf tip and margin whitish mildew like growth appears on leaves, which are killed or the dead area become dry.
if fruit is cracked a weft of fungus appear resulting in soft rot Etiology: Sporangiophores are slender, hyaline and branched, produce pear shaped sporangia with papilla.
Produces biflagellate zoospores.Antheridium is amphigynous and sexual spores are oospores.

pat301.t: Verticillium wilt - Verticillum dahliae, Verticillium albo-atrum
s: Verticillium wilt - Verticillum dahliae, Verticillium albo-atrum
Symptoms: Plants are stunted, leaves show dark green patches with interveinal and marginal yellowing.
Etiology: Conidiophores are vertically branched and conidia are single, cylindrical.
Mode of spread: Primary spread is through soil borne chlamydospores and dormant mycelium, secondary mycelium is through water borne conidia.
Bacterial wilt - Ralstonia solanacearum
Symptoms: Characteristic symptoms of bacterial wilt are the rapid and complete wilting of normal grown up plants.

in advantage cases, it may invade the cortex and pith and cause yellow brown discolouration of tissues and xylem blackening.Infected plant parts when cut and immersed in clear water, a white streak of bacterial
Mode of spread and survival: The bacterium survives in soil and they spread through irrigation water and by transplanting of infected seedlings.
Epidemiology: Relatively high soil moisture and soil temperature favour disease development.

pat301.t: Tomato spotted wilt disease (TSWV) OR Bronzy wilt
s: Tomato spotted wilt disease (TSWV) OR Bronzy wilt
Symptoms: Numerous small, dark, circular spots appear on younger leaves.
On ripe fruit, these markings are alternate bands of red and yellow.
Mode of spread: Tomato spotted wilt virus is transmitted through thrips (Thrips tabaci, Frankliniella schultzi and Frankliniella occidentalis).
Management: The affected plants should be removed and destroyed.

pat301.t: Phomopsis blight and fruit rot: Phomopsis vexans
s: Phomopsis blight and fruit rot: Phomopsis vexans
Leaf spots are clearly defined, circular, up to about 1 inch in diameter, and brown to gray with a narrow dark brown margin.
Fruit spots are much larger, affected fruit are first soft and watery but later may become black and mummified.
Pathogen Pycnidia with or without beak are found in the affected tissue.
Conidiophores in the pycnidium are hyaline, simple or branched.

pat301.t: Leaf spot: Cercospora solani -melongenae, C. solani
s: Leaf spot: Cercospora solani -melongenae, C. solani
Symptoms: The leaf spots are characterized by chlorotic lesions, angular to irregular in shape, later turn grayish-brown with profuse sporulation at the centre of the spot.
Conidiophores in mass are medium dark and slightly olivaceous brown in colour and paler towards the tip.
Mode of spread and survival The disease is spread by air borne conidia.
Management Pant Samrat variety is resistant to both the leaf spots.
Alternaria leaf spot - Alternaria melongenae
Several spots coalesce to form larger necrotic patches and later cause defoliation of leaves.
Large necrotic sunken spots develop on the fruits which turn yellow and drops.
The conidia are beaked, muriform, dark colored, with 5 - 10 transverse septa and a few longitudinal septa.
Management Nursery application with mancozeb 0.2% Difolatan 0.2% or captan 0.2% in the main field at intervals of 10 to 15 days reduces the disease incidence.
Bacterial wilt: Pseudomonas solanacearum/Ralstonia solanacearum
Symptoms The affected plants show yellowing of foliage, wilting and stunting of plants followed by death.
Mode of spread and survival The pathogen is soil borne and survives for several years in soil.
Epidemiology Humid weather and high temperature favour the disease.
Management Use resistant variety Pant samrat, Arka Nidhi, Arka Neelakantha,Surya and BB1 ,44 and 49.
Little leaf: Phytoplasmal diseases
Symptom The most characteristic symptom is the reduction in size of leaf.
The internodes get shortened and the axillary buds are stimulated to sprout and they grow into short branches, with very small leaves.
In the affected plants there will be no floral parts and if present they are modified in to green leaf like structures.
Fruit formation is very rare and the fruits formed are tough, leathery and may fail to mature normally.
Powdery mildew: Golvinomyces cichoracearum
Greyish powdery growth occurs on the under as well as on the upper surface of the leaf causing severe reduction in fruit yield.
Mode of spread and survival Air borne conidia spread the disease and the pathogen survives in the plant debris.
Management Spray wettable sulphur 0.25% or Dinocab (Karathane) 0.07%

pat301.t: Cercospora leaf spot: Cercospora abelmoschi ; Cercospora malayensis
s: Cercospora leaf spot: Cercospora abelmoschi ; Cercospora malayensis
Symptoms In India, two species of Cercospora produce leaf spots in bhendi.
Both the leaf spots cause severe defoliation and are common during humid seasons.
Mode of spread and survival Air borne conidia spread the disease and the pathogen survives in the plant debris.
Management Regular spraying with copper oxychloride 0.25% or Mancozeb 0.25% or Captan 0.1% reduces the incidence.

pat301.t: Fusarium wilt: Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. vasinfectum
s: Fusarium wilt: Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. vasinfectum

Symptoms The conspicuous symptom is a typical wilt, beginning with a yellowing and stunting of the plant, followed by wilting and rolling of the leaves as if the roots were unable to supply sufficient water.
If a diseased stem is split lengthwise, the vascular bundles appear as dark streaks.
When severely infected, nearly the whole stem is blackened.
Pathogen Macroconidia are 3- 5 septate formed on sporodochia and pionnotes.

pat301.t: Yellow vein mosaic: Bhendi Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus
s: Yellow vein mosaic: Bhendi Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus
Symptoms Yellowing of the entire network of veins in the leaf blade is the characteristic symptom.
In severe infections the younger leaves turn yellow, become reduced in size and the plant is highly stunted.
Mode of spread and survival The virus is transimtted by Bemisia tabaci.
Survive on weed host croton sparsiflorus Management Take up vector control by using Nuvan and Dimecron Starting from 7 DAS and repeat every 15 days.
Club root - Plasmodiophora brassicae (Woronin)
Symptoms: The above-ground plant parts show stunting, reduction in the size of head leaves shown pale green to yellowish.
When such plants are pulled out and the roots examined, the roots are malformed into spherical, knobby and club-like structures.
Mode of spread and survival: The pathogen is capable of surviving in the soil for 7-10 years as resting spores.
The resting spores of the fungus can be spread from field to field by infested soil, contaminated water supplies, infected transplants, farm machinery and animals.
Black spot - Alternaria brassicae
Symptoms: Small, brown to black circular spots appear on older leaves.
Mode of spread and survival: Pathogens are seed borne or the conidia are borne abundantly in moist atmosphere and are disseminated readily by air currents.
Epidemiology: Rain or dew that persists for more than 9 hours is required for germination and infection to occur.
Excessive irrigation should be avoided and good weed control maintained.
Downy mildew - Hyaloperonospora brassicae
Symptoms: The fungus when attacks the young seedlings, discoloration occurs and in severe cases the whole plant perishes.
Purplish leaf spots or yellow brown spots on the upper surface of the leaf appear, while fluffy downy fungus growth is found on the lower surface.
Etiology : Sporangiophores are dichotomously branched at acute angles.
Mode of spread and survival: The fungus perennates in the soil through oospores in roots or in old diseased plant parts and as contaminant with seeds.

pat301.t: Black leg - Leptosphaeria maculans (Anamorph: Phoma lingam)
s: Black leg - Leptosphaeria maculans (Anamorph: Phoma lingam)
Symptoms: Fungus attacks the crop at seedling or at any stage.
Mode of spread and survival: Pathogen can survive for up to four years in seed and three years in infected crop debris.
The pathogen infects seedlings, forms pycnidia and produces abundant amounts of spores and are splashed to nearby plants to initiate new infections.
Secondary infection is through water and primary infection is through Ascospores.

pat301.t: Yellows - Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. conglutinans
s: Yellows - Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. conglutinans
Plants which do not die are often stunted and have one-sided yellowing of the leaves.
Mode of survival and spread: This fungus survives in the soil and produces spores which can persist in the soil for many years.
Epidemiology: The disease is generally favoured by warm soil temperatures above 20°C.
Management: Resistant varieties help provide the most effective control of this disease.

pat301.t: Root rot or wire stem - Rhizoctonia solani
s: Root rot or wire stem - Rhizoctonia solani
Symptoms: Young plants show soft, water soaked lesion on the stem near soil level, the cotyledons wither and the plant eventually fall over and perishes.

When infection occurs at a later stage of growth, the lower part shows discoloration over a length of several centimeters, becomes hard and woody and thinner than usual as the cortical tissue dies and this phen
Management: Seed treatment with Captan or Thiram 4g/kg, followed by Trichoderma viride 4g/kg.
Seedbed drenches with Copper oxychloride 0.25% will give good disease control.

pat301.t: White blisters or Rust of raddish: Albugo candida
s: White blisters or Rust of raddish: Albugo candida
Systemic infection When young stems and flowering parts are infected it becomes systemic.
Young stem and inflorescence are infected and cause deformities like swelling and distortions due to hypertrophy and hyperplasia.
The petals and sepals are modified into leaf like structure and results in sterility of the ovary.
Mode of spread and survival: The disease spreads primarily by germination of oospore and secondary spread is by zoospores.

pat301.t: Black rot - Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris
s: Black rot - Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris
The disease occurs on cabbage, cauliflower, turnip, Brussels sporut, broccoli, knol knol, raddish, mustard and other cruciferous plants.
Symptoms: The first sign of the disease is the occurrence of chlorotic lesions near the leaf margin, which progresses towards the center in the form of V-shaped yellowish spots.
The vein and veinlets turn brown and finally black, which is characteristic of the disease.
Pathogen: The bacterium is a rod with single polar flagellum.
Cauliflower mosaic virus (CaMV)
Symptoms: CaMV induces a variety of systemic symptoms such as mosaic, necrotic lesions on leaf surfaces, stunted growth and deformation of the overall plant structure.
Mode of spread: CaMV is transmitted in a non-circulatory manner by aphid, Myzus persicae.
Once introduced within a plant host cell, virions migrate to the nuclear envelope of the plant cell.
Black Rot: Ceratocystis fimbriata
Symptoms Small, circular, slightly sunken, dark brown spots are the initial symptoms of black rot.
Spots enlarge and appear greenish black to black when wet and grayish black when dry.
Within the spots are small, black fungal structures (perithecia) with long necks which appear to the naked eye as dark bristles.
Do not wash and package roots showing symptoms of black rot.
Rhizophus soft rot: Rhizopus stolonifer
Symptoms Infection and decay commonly occur at one or both ends of the root, although infection occasionally begins elsewhere.
If the humidity is high, the sweet potatoes become heavily "whiskered" with a grayish black fungal growth.
The colour of the root is not significantly altered, but an odour is produced that attracts fruit flies to the area.
Infection is especially likely if the relative humidity is between 75 and 85 percent during storage or transport.

pat301.t: White rust/ Blister - Albugo ipomoea - panduratae
s: White rust/ Blister - Albugo ipomoea - panduratae
Symptoms: Presence of chlorotic or yellowish blotches, initially round to angular where they are limited by veins, on the upper surface of leaves.
On the lower surface, white creamy pustules produced corresponding upper surface yellow discolouration.
Bacterial soft rot: Erwinia chrysanthemi
Symptoms Roots are affected in the field, or more commonly in storage, by a soft rot that turns diseased tissue light brown and watery.
Some storage roots appear healthy from the outside but are decayed internally.
Management Carefully handle sweet potatoes during all stages of production.
This is the most important control method for bacterial soft rot.

pat301.t: Halo Blight of Bean: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola
s: Halo Blight of Bean: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola
Symptoms: Characteristic symptoms are formed on the stem, leaf petioles, pods, seeds and on seedlings.
Initially, the lesions appear as water-soaked area, and as the spots dry out, a reddish margin is developed.
Sometimes, deep cracks are formed in the stem, through which the bacterial exudate comes out.
The seeds inside the infected pods may get infected and become small, wrinkled and are yellowish in colour.

pat301.t: Basal stem rot /Thanjavur wilt - Ganoderma lucidum
s: Basal stem rot /Thanjavur wilt - Ganoderma lucidum
Symptoms Susceptible stage 10-30 years On Stem Diseased palm shows exudation of reddish brown, viscous liquid from the basal portion of the stem up to 3-5 meters.
On Inflorescence and nuts In the diseased trees development of flower is arrested and button shedding can be commonly seen.
On Roots Decay and death of finer roots precede bleeding symptoms in the stem.
The disease spreads to other roots and may show rotting of 70% of the total roots.
Bud Rot- Phytophthora palmivora
The affected heart leaf comes off easily when it is pulled.
When the growing bud is affected the tree is killed Pathogen The fungus produces intercellur, non septate, hyaline mycelium.
The sporangiophores are hyaline, Thin walled, pear shaped with a prominent papillae.
In addition, thick walled, yellowish brown chlamydospores are also produced.
Stem bleeding - Theilaviopsis paradoxa (Ceratocystis paradoxa)
Symptoms The characteristic symptom is the exudation of reddish brown fluid from the cracks in the stem.
As the disease progresses, more area underneath the bark gets decayed and the bleeding patch extends further up.
The vigour of the tree is affected and nut yield is reduced.
The tree is not killed outright but become uneconomical to maintain.

pat301.t: Gray leaf Spot (or) Blight: Pestalotiopsis palmarum
s: Gray leaf Spot (or) Blight: Pestalotiopsis palmarum
Symptoms The disease symptoms develop on the outer whorl of leaves.
Symptoms appear first as minute yellow spots encircled by a greyish band on the leaflets.
On the upper leaf surface globose (or) rectangular (or) ovoid black minute acervuli of the fungus are formed.
The acervuli are black in colour, cushion shaped and sub epidermal and break open to expose conidia and black sterile structures, setae.

pat301.t: Root wilt / Kerala wilt: Mycoplasma - like Organism (MLO)
s: Root wilt / Kerala wilt: Mycoplasma - like Organism (MLO)
The disease is seen only in older palms, (Palms up to an age of 2 years are not affected).
Symptoms First symptom appears on leaves of middle whorl and extends to outer whorl.
they curve abnormally inwards, resembling the ribs of mammals) of leaf lets are the most characteristic symptoms.
Newly formed leaves are small, the buttons and tender nuts shed off.
Tatipaka disease: Unknown etiology
Symptoms Tapering of the stem below the crown is one of the characteristic features of the disease.
Diseased tress show twisted trunk (or) 'S' shaped bend in trunk below the crown.
The leaves in the infected trees leaves become small and slowly turn yellowish green.
In extreme cases of tatipaka disease, the palms do not produce any nuts.

pat301.t: Mahali disease: (or) Koleroga (Kota-rotling ; roga disease): Phytophthora arecae
s: Mahali disease: (or) Koleroga (Kota-rotling ; roga disease): Phytophthora arecae
Symptoms The disease is very common in heavy rainfall area.
Water soaked lesion appear on nuts resulting in rotting and excessive shedding of immature nuts.
Lesions cover entire nuts and fruit stalk & inflorescence rachis are also affected.

Mode of spread and survival The pathogen survives in affected nuts and rain plays a major role in spread Epidemiology Low temperature and high humidity favour the growth of the fungus Management Spray 1% Bordea

pat301.t: Anbe roga or basal rot- Ganoderma lucidum
s: Anbe roga or basal rot- Ganoderma lucidum
Symptoms Yellowing of leaves Leaves dry, droop and fall - off Stem brittle and easily breaks Oozing of dark fluid.
Pathogen : Produces basidiocarp with stipe Mode off spread: Primary Rhizomorph aand secondary Basidiospores Lecture 15- DISEASES OF TEA DISEASES CAUSAL ORGANISM 1.

FUNGAL DISEASES Blister blight Exobasidium vexans Pink disease Pellicularia salmonicolor Grey blight Pestalotia theae Black rot Corticium invisum(Rosellina arcuta) Armillariella root rot Armillariella mellea Re
Blister blight: Exobasidium vexans
Symptoms The first visible symptom is an oily, yellowish, translucent spot on the tender leaf which turn to deep red shiny blisters.
Pathogen The mycelium is confined to the blistered areas on the leaves.
They are septae and collect in bundles below the lower epidermis.
Later by rupturing the epidermis continuous layer of vertical hyphae are projected on the surface of spot.
Pink disease: Pellicularia salmonicolor
Symptoms First a number of fine silky threads get united into thin film forms pink fructifications over affected stem.
They are generally confined to lower or more shady side of branches.
When the branch increases in thickness it grows only in areas where bark is not dead.
Mode of spread and survival Basidiospores are wind borne.
Grey blight: Pestalotia theae
Symptoms The disease appears as minute brownish spots on older leaves, which soon turn grey.
The spots are mostly irregular and several of them may coalesce to form irregular grey patches.
Epidemiology The incidence is more frequent on weak bushes especially if potassium is deficient.
The disease is also predisposed by sun scorch, insect puncture and plucking wounds.
Black root: Corticium invisum
Symptoms: Black strands adhere to the roots as loose cob-webby mass star like sheets of white mycelium on the collar region.
Mode of spread and survival: The disease develops rapidly when temperature is high and air is humid.
Management Prune the crop in December and collect all dead leaves, dried leaves and burn.
Red Rust: Cephaleuros mycoides
Symptoms Small translucent water soaked spots appear on leaf.
On the under surface it is purple red and become grey brown when old.
Mode of spread and survival Sporangia are spread by wind or rain Epidemiology Weakness due to lack of drainage, shallow soil, hard pan, poor soil, hard plucking, improper pruning etc.
Too severe pruning of young plants, weakening by red spider attack, drought and logging also favour the disease.
Armillaria root rot - Armillaria mellea
Symptoms: Bushes wilt and turn chlorotic, affect collar region ;
Bark cracks Sheets of creamy coloured mycelium accompanied by flattened brown rhizomorph Sphorophores produced on collar region death of whole plants.
Mode of spread Primary and Secondary spread through Rhizomorph and root contact.
Lecture 16- DISEASES OF COFFEE DISEASES CAUSAL ORGANISM 1.
Leaf rust - Hemiliea vastatrix
Symptoms Small yellowish, translucent oily spots appear on 12 week old young leaves.
In severe attacks leaves are completely defoliated and berries remain small.
Pathogen The mycelium is intercellular and sends haustoria into the cells.
The uredospores are reniform or orange segment like in shape.
Anthracnose: Glomerella cingulata
Symptoms Greenish spots on appear on leaves, twigs and berries.
Spots are also observed on the internodes of twigs resulting in blackened twigs and begin to die from tip to downwards.
Mode of spread Wind-borne conidia spread the pathogen aand ascospores from dried fallen leaves.
Epidemiology Dry period followed by the monsoon rain favour the disease development.
Brown eye spot: Cercospora coffeicola
Symptoms The disease is severe on nursery seedlings and young crop.
Small circular necrotic spots with a dark brown margin and light brown centre occur on the leaves.
Made of spread The pathogen is seed borne, conidia spread by wind.
Epidemiology Ill-nourished, unshaded crop at low altitudes favour disease development.
Black rot: Corticium salmonicolor
In south India the disease is severe only in those areas growing with C.
It is influenced by south west monsoon period from June - Sep.
Symptoms The disease is characterized by blackening of the affected leaves, twigs and berries.
The under surface of the affected leaves is covered by a thin hyaline spreading web of fungal mycelium.
Abnormal leaf fall : Phytophthora palmivora
Symptoms Grey circular spots appear on leaves and these spots enlarge and become irregular, turn reddish brown and fall off.
The affected branches shows die back symptom and there will be reduction in latex yield.
Pathogen: Sexual spores are oospores and chlamydospores are resting spores Mode of spread and survival The fungus survives in infected fruits during dry season.

Epidemiology Moist climate with intermittent rainfall, temperature below 28.9oc, RH above 90 per cent, rain fall at least 2.5mm per day and sun shine at least 3hrs per day are the favourable factors for the dev
Powdery mildew: Oidium heveae
Symptoms: White powdery growth appears on upper surface and the affected leaves turn purplish black.
Petioles alone remain to the twigs giving broom stick appearance.
Mode of spread and survival The pathogen spreads through wind borne conidia.

The pathogen survives in the infested debris Epidemiology Cloudy days with light rains and or misty nights with dew formation, during defoliation encourage the disease development Management Spraying wettable S
Pink disease: Corticium salmonicolor
Mode of Survival and spread: Survive in affected plant parts.
Primary infection is through wind born spores Epidemiology Infection is noticed during south west monsoon period, but visible effects are mostly noticed from august to September onwards.
Pink diseases are noticed in all stages but mostly 12 years old crop are affected.
Management: Cut ends should be protected with Bordeaux paste (or) Painting tar on the affected portion Lecture 17-DISEASES OF COCOA DISEASES CAUSAL ORGANISM 1.
Black pod disease - Phytophthora palmivora
Symptoms First sign of the disease is the appearance of brown spot on the pod.
Mode of spread and survival The fungus persists as dormant mycelium and as chlamydospores.
The pathogen is disseminated by windborne spores, wind splashed rains and insects.
Epidemiology The disease spreads rapidly under conditions of high rainfall and long periods of high humidity.

pat301.t: Swollen shoot - Cocoa swollen shoot virus / Cocoa mottle leaf virus
s: Swollen shoot - Cocoa swollen shoot virus / Cocoa mottle leaf virus
Symptoms Swelling developed on nodes, internodes and tips of the quick growing shoots.
As the leaves enlarge, the red pattern is joined by chlorotic or transparent lesion.
Mode of spread The virus is spread by insect especially mealy bugs and by grafting.
Management Field sanitation and vector control helps to check the disease.

pat301.t: Panama wilt disease: Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense
s: Panama wilt disease: Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense
Economic Importance The first major disease which attacked banana was called Panama disease from the area where it first became serious.
Banana wilt is a soil-borne fungal disease and gets entry in the plant body through roots and wounds caused by nematodes.
Symptoms Yellowing of the lower most leaves occur and yellowing extends upwards, droop off and finally heart leaf alone remain green and erect.
Etiology The fungal hyphae is both inter and intra cellular and Micro,Macro conidia and Chlamydospores Mode of spread and survival The pathogen survives in soil as chlamydospores for longer periods.

pat301.t: Sigatoka leaf spot : Cercospora musae (Mycosphaerella musicola)
s: Sigatoka leaf spot : Cercospora musae (Mycosphaerella musicola)
Symptoms Two types of leaf spots Yellow leaf spot - Mycosphaerella musicola Black leaf spot - Mycosphaerella fijiensis First symptoms are seen on the leaves as yellow elongated spots.
Pathogen The conidia are narrow and tapering, contain numerous transverse septa.

Mode of spread and survival The fungus survives in the infected banana leaves, Primary infection through ascospores from infected plant debris and secondary infection by windborne conidia spread the disease.
Rapid spread of sigatoka disease and heavy infection are favoured by worm temperature (23-25oC),rainy or humid weather.

pat301.t: Anthracnose and fruit rot - Gloeosporium gloeosporioides
s: Anthracnose and fruit rot - Gloeosporium gloeosporioides
Symptoms: The skin at the distal ends of the fingers turns black.
The entire fruit, stalk and buds are affected, the bunch becomes black and fruits get shriveled.
Pathogen Acervuli are usually rounded or sometimes elongated, erumpent.
Conidiophores are cylindrical, tapered towards the apex, hyaline and septate.

pat301.t: Freckle leaf spot/ Black spot- Phyllostictina musarum
s: Freckle leaf spot/ Black spot- Phyllostictina musarum
Symptoms Minute black spots appear on leaves and fruits.
The spots are brown to dark brown initially.On centre of spot pycnidia are present.
On the fruits the pathogen is confined to only to the skin.
Mode of Spread Pycnidium and the pycnidiospores are disseminated by wind.
Moko wilt: Ralstonia solanacearum (Pseudomonas solanacearum)
Symptoms ◦ Rapid wilting and collapse of the leaves are the main symptoms.
◦ Blackening of the suckers, discolouration of fruits, reddish tinge in vascular strand are the typical symptoms of this disease.
Etiology It is gram negative ,bacillus bacteria, motile with polar flagella.
It is an obligate aerobe Mode of Spread and survival The disease occurs in poorly drained soil.

pat301.t: Banana bunchy top: Banana bunchy top virus or Musa virus 1
s: Banana bunchy top: Banana bunchy top virus or Musa virus 1
Dark broken bands of green tissues can be seen on the veins, leaves and petioles.
Etiology It is referred as BBTV, a circular, single stranded DNA virus.
Mode of spread The disease is transmitted primarily by infected suckers.
Secondary spread is through the black aphid vector Pentalonia nigronervosa.
Banana bract mosaic:
Greenish to brownish spindle-shaped streaks irregularly scattered along leaf petioles.

Pinkish spindle shaped lesions at the base of pseudostem, loosening of leaf sheath and appear like travellers palm Vector: Aphids - Aphis gossypii Pathogen: Banana Bract mosaic virus, flexible rod shaped ssRNA
Damping Off - Pythium aphanidermatum
Symptoms Sprouting seedlings are infected and wither before emergence from the soil [Pre-emergence damping off].
Water soaked minute lesions appear on the stem near the soil surface, Stem gridled and spreads up and down in the stem and the seedlings topple over [Post-emergence damping off].
The young seedlings in the nursery are killed in patches.
Etiology Zoospores are kidney shaped and biflagellate and Zoospores are produced from sporangia.

pat301.t: Black Shank - Phytophthora parasitica var. nicotianae
s: Black Shank - Phytophthora parasitica var. nicotianae
Symptoms Seedlings in the nursery and in main field show black discolouration of the stem near the soil level and blackening of roots.

Affected leaves wither and tips dry and may produce blighting and drying of the bottom leaves - Finally blackening and rotting of the leaves occur.When affected stem is split open the pith region is found to be
Etiology The sporangia are hyaline, pyriform with papillae, developing from sporangiophores in sympodial branches.
Frog Eye Spot - Cercospora nicotianae
Symptoms The disease appear mostly on matured, lower leaves as small ashy grey spots with brown border.
The typical spots have a white centre, surrounded in succession by grey and brown portions and a dark brown to black margin, resembling the eyes of a frog.
Several spots coalesce and become irregular causing drying of the affected tissues.
Etiology The mycelium is intercellular which aggregates beneath the epidermis and produce cluster of conidiophores which emerge through stomata.
Wild Fire - Pseudomonas tabaci
Symptoms Dark brown to black spots with a yellow halo develops and spreads quickly causing withering and drying of leaves.
In advanced cases, lesions develop on the young stem, leading to withering and drying of the seedlings.
Finally, the entire leaf is fully covered with enlarged spots with yellow halos and show blighted appearance.
Etiology The bacterium produces a fluroscent pigment and potent toxin Tabtoxin or wildfire toxin.
Mosaic - Tobacco mosaic virus [TMV]
vulgare Symptoms The leaves develop characteristic light and dark green patches.
In severe cases, the leaves are narrowed, puckered, become thin and malformed beyond recognition.

Later, dark brown necrotic spots develop under hot weather and this symptom is called as '' mosaic burn'' or ''mosaic scorching'' Etiology Rod shaped measuring 300× 150-180µm and contains Ribonucleic acid with
Mode of Spread and Survival The virus is contagious and sap transmissible.

pat301.t: Broom Rape - Orobanche cernua and O.indica
s: Broom Rape - Orobanche cernua and O.indica
It is an annual, fleshy flowering plant with a short stem.
The stem is pale yellow in colour and covered by brown scaly leaves and 10-15 cm height.
Symptoms The young shoot of the parasite emerges from the soil at the base of the plants at 5-6 weeks after transplanting.
The affected tobacco plants are stunted and show withering and drooping of leaves leading to wilting Disease cycle Primary infection occurs from the seeds in the soil.
Anthracnose: Colletotrichum spp.

Symptoms Yellowish brown depressed spots on stem later turns to brown and Black Stem girdling, wilting of plants and produces poor pods Pathogen Cushion shaped acervulus is seen below epidermis or cuticle with
Setae - septate, stout at base and pointed at tip, dark brown, long, present in the periphery or in between the conidiophores.
Conidiophores - simple, elongate, septate, hyaline to brown, Conidia- sickle shaped, , guttulate ( oil globule ), hyaline, single celled.
Stem gall - Protomyces spp.
It produces small greenish galls on the lower stem which turn to dark brown and crack at maturity.
Diseases of Mulberry Diseases Causal organism Powdery mildew Phyllactinia corylea Leaf rust Peridiospora mori Leaf spot Cercospora moricola Sooty mould Capnodium spp.
DOWNY MILDEW/GREEN EAR - Sclerospora graminicola
Symptoms The first symptom appears in seedlings at 3-4 leaf stage.
The affected ear is transformed in to green leafy structure hence the name "green ear" disease.
Mostly the entire ear is transformed in to leafy structures, but at times a part of the ear also affected and the other parts produce normal grains.
As the disease advance, the green leafy structures become brown and dry.
ERGOT/SUGARY DISEASE - Claviceps fusiformis
Symptoms The disease occurs only at the time of flowering.
Mode of spread and Survival The honey dew attracts insects and ants which help in secondary spreading of the disease.
The pathogen survives as Sclerotia in soil which is viable for 6-8 months.
Epidemiology High relative humidity (85-95%), Cloudy weather and intermittent raining for 5-6 days during flowering stage encourage the disease.
SMUT - Tolyposporium penicillariae
Symptoms The pathogen infects the florets and transforms them into large sacs containing black powder of smut spores.
Mode of spread and survival The pathogen is soil borne and survives as spore balls in soil.
These spore balls germinate to give rise sporidia which are carried by wind and effects the secondary infection.
Epidemiology High humidity and successive cropping of pearl millet favours the disease development.
RUST - Puccinia penniseti
Symptoms The disease first appears on the older leaves as pustules containing reddish brown uredospores.

Life cycle Uredial and telial stages are completed on cumbu and Aecial and pycnidial stages are completed on brinjal (Alternate host) Mode of spread and survival The pathogen spreads through air borne uredospor
Epidemiology Rainy weather and low temperature encourage the disease development.
Management Spray with captafol 1 kg/ha or mancozeb 1.25 kg/ha Grow resistant varieties like IP 537-B, P - 2890, 1577, 1581 and 2880
Red rust: Cephaleuros virescens
It is an algal parasite Symptom The disease affects leaves and fruits.
Produce small red to orange velvety mycelial growth on upper surface of leaves.
Epidemiology Bright sunlight favour the disease Management Spray Bordeaux mixture 0.6% or Copper oxychloride 0.2 to 0.3%.

pat301.t: Foot or stem rot : Pythium aphanidermatum
s: Foot or stem rot : Pythium aphanidermatum
Symptom This pathogen also causes damping off in nursery.
Drench the soil with 1% Bordeaux mixture or copper oxychloride 0.25%.
Leaf spot
Symptom Round irregular oval or elongated spots appear on the leaves.
The spots are white in centre bounded by yellowish or brownish margin.
Mode of spread and survival The pathogen spreads through wind and survives in plant debris Management Three spraying with 1% Bordeaux mixture controls the disease.
Powdery mildew: Oidium caricae
Flower stalks and fruits are also affected and exhibit white powdery patches Pathogen Obligate parasite produces short conidiophore and also produces haustoria.
Barrel shaped conidia, mycelium hyaline septate conidiophore short hyaline and produces conidia in chains.
Mode of spread Primary: Soil borne ascospores Secondary: Wind borne conidia
Anthracnose: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides
Symptoms Spots seen on leaves and fruits Leaf : Necrotic spots on leaf Fruit : Circular, slightly sunken spots.
Latex oozes out Pathogen Hemi biotroph produces hyaline septate branched mycelia.
Conidia are single celled, hyaline, thin walled with full of oil globules.
Mode of spread Primary spread and Secondary spread through wind borne conidia

pat301.t: Papaya ring spot: Papaya Ring Spot Virus
s: Papaya ring spot: Papaya Ring Spot Virus
Symptoms Vein clearing, puckering or bulging of leaf tissues between veins.
Margin and distal parts of leaves roll downward and inwards, mosaic mottling, dark green blisters, leaf distortion which result in shoe string system and stunting of plants.
Pathogen: PRSV is a flexious rod shaped RNA virus belongs to potyvirus group transmitted by Aphids in a non- persistant manner Vector : Aphids Aphis gossypii & A.

pat301.t: Leaf curl - Tobacco Leaf Curl Virus
s: Leaf curl - Tobacco Leaf Curl Virus
Symptoms Curling, crinkling and distortion of leaves, reduction of leaf lamina, rolling of leaf margins inward and downward, thickening of veins.
Causal organism: Papaya Leaf curl virus (PLCV) is a DNA virus in the family Geminiviridae.
Anthracnose: Gloeosporium gloeosporioides
Symptoms Spots seen on leaves and fruits Leaf : Necrotic spots on leaf Fruit : Circular, slightly sunken spots .Latex oozes out Pathogen: Hemi biotroph produces hyaline septate branched mycelia.
Conidia are single celled, hyaline, thin walled with full of oil globules.
Mode of spread Primary spread and Secondary spread through wind borne conidia
Cercospora leaf spot: Cercospora punicae
Symptoms Light brown zonate sports appear on leaves and fruits Black elliptical spots appear on the twigs Affected areas in the twigs become flattened and depressed with raised edge.
Pathogen: Conidiophore are olivaceous brown, short fasciculate, sparingly septate.
Mode of spread Primary spread through ascospores from fallen leaves and Secondary spread is through wind borne conidia

pat301.t: Bacterial leaf spot: Xanthomonas campestris pv. punicae
s: Bacterial leaf spot: Xanthomonas campestris pv. punicae
Symptoms Dark coloured irregular spots 2-5 mm in diameter The leaves often distorted and malformed Premature dropping of leaves.
The normal growth of the plant in affected Raised spots are seen on the fruits which are irregular.
Pathogen: Gram negative, rot, motile with single polar flagella Mode of spread & Survival The bacteria infect through wounds and stomatal openings.

pat301.t: DOWNY MILDEW OR CRAZY TOP- Sclerophthora macrospora
s: DOWNY MILDEW OR CRAZY TOP- Sclerophthora macrospora
Philippine downy mildew - Perenosclerospora philippinensis Sorghum downy mildew - Peronosclerospora sorghi Downy mildew of maize disease was reported by Butler and Bisby (1933) in India.
Symptoms The development of chlorotic streaks appears on the leaves and plants exhibit stunted and bushy appearance due to shortening of internodes.
Later browning of tissues and leaf shredding symptoms are noticed.
Etiology Survives as oospores (resting spore) in host tissue and soil.
CHARCOAL ROT - Macrophomina phaseolina
Symptoms After flowering, intial symptoms are the abnormal drying of upper leaf tissues.
The fungus attack roots of seedlings and young plants [wilt symptom].
Etiology Pycndiospores are hyaline, rod and single celled and borne in black flask shaped pycnidia.
Mode of spread The primary infection takes place through the sclerotia present in the soil and the secondary spread is through wind borne pycnidiospores and soil.
Head SMUT - Sphacelotheca reiliana
the fungus penetrates the seedlings and grows inside the plant without showing symptoms, until the tasselling and silking stage.
Finally the tassel wholly gets converted in to smut sorus .
Etiology Teliospores can survive for several years in soil .

pat301.t: Common smut - Ustilago maydis (Ustilago means burn)
s: Common smut - Ustilago maydis (Ustilago means burn)
Symptoms When young corn seedlings are infected, minute galls form on the leaves and stems and the seedlings may remain stunted or may be killed.
On older plants, infected areas are permeated by fungus mycelium which stimulates the host cells to divide and enlarge, thus forming galls.
Galls are first covered with greenish white membrane they reach a size of 1-15cm in diameter and turns into olive-brown spores.
Etiology The fungus produces dikaryotic mycelium .Teliospores are black, ellipsoidal .

pat301.t: Turcicum Leaf Blight - Exserohilum turcicum (Helminthosporium turcicum)
s: Turcicum Leaf Blight - Exserohilum turcicum (Helminthosporium turcicum)
Symptoms Small yellowish round to oval spots on lower leaves develops which later turns greyish brown colour in the centre with dark brown margins.
The surface is covered with olive green velvety masses of conidia and conidiophores.
Etiology Conidiophores are in group, geniculate, mid dark brown, pale near the apex and smooth.
Conidia are distinctly curved, fusiform, and pale to golden brown with 5-11 pseudosepta.
RUST- Puccinia sorghi
Symptoms Minute, Circular to oval elongated, reddish brown powdery pustules (uredia) can be seen scattered over both surfaces of leaves.
The pustules are yellowish in early stages and later become as red uredospores to black teliospores Etiology Heteroceious, Uredospores single celled , echinucleate, yellowish brown.
Mode of spread and survival The fungus spreads through wind borne urediniospores and survives in the alternate hosts Epidemiology Cool temperature and high RH encourages the disease.
Management Remove alternate host Spray mancozeb @ 2.5g/ lit.
Maize Streak virus (MSV)
Symptoms: Maize plants infected within 3 weeks of emergence become stunted and may die early or produce small poorly filled ears.
The main symptom is broken to almost continuous, narrow chlorotic streaks centred on leaf veins.
BLAST - Pyricularia setariae
Symptoms The spots present on the leaf blade are circular with light centre and are surrounded by a dark brown margin.
Mode of spread The pathogen spreads through air borne conidia Survival The pathogen survives in the infected plant debris and collateral hosts.

Epidemiology High RH, low night temperature and cloudy weather favours the disease development Management Seed treatment with captan or thiram @ 4 g/kg or carbendazim 2 g/kg of seed Spray the crop with Iprobenp
LEAF SPOT/LEAF BLOTCH - Helminthosporium setariae
Symptoms Spots of varying sizes viz., small, large and brown coloured are formed on the leaves.
Lesions also appear as blotches and rotting of the secondary roots also occurs.

Mode of spread The pathogen is externally seed borne Survival The pathogen survive in the infected seeds Epidemiology A temperature of 300 C is ideal for the disease development Management Seed treatment with c
HEAD SMUT - Sorosporium paspali-thunbergii
Symptoms The entire panicle is transformed in to a long sorus and a young cream coloured thin membrane covers the sorus.

Later the membrane bursts open and exposes the black mass of spores Mode of spread and survival The pathogen is seed borne and survives in the infected grains Management Seed treatment with captan or thiram @ 4
TIKKA LEAF SPOT
On the lower surface, the lesions are light brown in colour.
Conidiophores is olivaceous or yellowish brown in colour, short and 1 or 2 septate Conidia are often curved 3-12 septate.
Tikka late leaf spot - Phaeoisariopsis personata (Cercospora personata) The late leaf spot disease appears 5-7 weeks after sowing.
Late leaf spot attack in usually coincides with rust disease.
RUST - Puccinia arachidis
Rust is now considered as an economically important disease in almost all groundnut growing areas of the world Symptoms Infection occurs on 6 weeks old crop.
Orange coloured pustules (uredosori) appear on the lower surface of the leaves and ruptures, release masses of reddish brown uredospores.
Severe infection leads to production of small and shriveled seeds.

pat301.t: CROWN ROT/COLLAR ROT -Aspergillus niger and A. flavus
s: CROWN ROT/COLLAR ROT -Aspergillus niger and A. flavus
Symptoms Pre emergence- Rotting of seed , germination affected Post emergence- Circular brown spots on cotyledons of seedlings.
The infected areas become water-soaked and turn light brown and are soon covered with black fungal spores [sooty like appearance].
The fungus sporulate on the surface of mature pods resulting in patches of black sooty spores.

pat301.t: STEM AND POD ROT - Sclerotoum rolfsii
s: STEM AND POD ROT - Sclerotoum rolfsii
Symptoms The first symptom of stem rot are yellowing and wilting of branches near the base of the plant.
Sheets of white mycelium develop at or near the soil line around the affected areas of the stem which become shredded.
BACTERIAL WILT - Pseudomonas solanacearum
Symptoms Infection of young plants results in rapid wilting of stem and foliage.
Infection of mature plants results in loss of turgidity and leaves become light green, chlorotic and curl at the tips.
The characteristic symptom are dark brown discolouration in the xylem and pith and the streaming of ''bacterial ooze'' from the cut ends of infected root and stem.
Mode of spread Seed borne inoculum spreads the disease Survival Long term survival of the pathogen is favoured by continuous cropping of susceptible host.

pat301.t: Bud necrosis/ peanut spotted wilt virus - Tomato spotted wilt virus [TSWV]
s: Bud necrosis/ peanut spotted wilt virus - Tomato spotted wilt virus [TSWV]
It is also called as Ring mosaic, groundnut mosaic, bunchy top, chlorosis, ring mottle and bud blight.
Symptoms Initial symptoms appear on young leaflets as chlorotic spots.
The seeds produced by the infected plants are small, shriveled ,rugosity and mottled.
transmits the disease Pathogenic characters Groundnut bud necrosis virus are spherical, 30 nm in diameter, ssRNA with multipartite genome.
LEAF BLIGHT - Alternaria sesami
Symptoms Small circular, reddish brown spots [1-8 mm] appear on leaves which enlarge later with concentric rings.
Lesions may coalesce to form large necrotic areas and defoliation usually results.
In severe blighting dark brown lesions can be seen on petiole, stem and capsules.
Infection of capsules results in pre mature splitting with shriveled and poorly mature seeds.
ROOT ROT/CHARCOAL ROT - Macrophomina phaseolina
Charcoal rot of sesame is very destructive and present in all the sesame growing areas Symptoms The pathogen attacks the stem at the collar region.
The symptoms include yellowing of lower leaves (collar region), drooping and defoliation.
Inside the affected stem and roots numerous black sclerotia can be seen and the diseased plants can be pulled out very easily from the soil.
POWDERY MILDEW - Erysiphe cichoracearum
Symptoms Small, white powdery growth appears on the upper surface of leaves and in severe cases, the spots coalesce and the entire leaf surface becomes covered with powdery coating.
The infection may be seen on the flowers and young capsules, leading to premature shredding.
Mode of spread Spreads through wind borne conidia Survival The pathogen survives in the infected plant debris Epidemiology Dry humid weather and low RH favour the disease.

Management Remove and destroy the infected plant debris Application of sulphur dust @ 25 kg/ha or spraying wettable sulphur @ 2.5 kg/ha Grow resistant cultivars like Si 44, 68, 71, 250, 1157, 1167, EC 20804, 20
PHYLLODY - Phytoplasma [MLO]
Symptoms The plants bear cluster of leaves and malformed flowers at the tip.
Infected floral parts are transformed in to green leafy structures, which grow profusely.
The plant is stunted with reduced internodes and abnormal branching, gives a bushy appearance.
The most characteristic symptom of the disease is transformation of flower parts in to green leaf-like structure.
SEEDLING BLIGHT - Phytophthora parasitica
Symptoms The disease appears as circular, dull green patch on both the surface of the cotyledonary leaves.

Infected stem show black discolouration and severe defoliation Mode of spread and survival The pathogen spreads through wind borne sporangia and survives in seeds and as oospores in soil Epidemiology Cool and m

RUST - Melampsora ricini
Symptoms Minute, orange-yellow coloured, raised pustules appear with powdery masses on the lower surface of the leaves.
Pustules are grouped in concentric rings and drying of leaves results.
LEAF BLIGHT - Alternaria ricini
Symptoms In leaves, irregular brown spots with concentric rings, variable in size appear which are usually surrounded by yellow halos.
In severe cases, the stem, capsules, and inflorescence also show dark brown lesions and premature defoliation occurs.

pat301.t: BACTERIAL LEAF BLIGHT - Xanthomonas campestris pv. ricini
s: BACTERIAL LEAF BLIGHT - Xanthomonas campestris pv. ricini
Symptoms Water soaked lesions appear, which later become brown/black and angular to circular in shape.
Later the affected leaves become brittle, dry up, drop prematurely and defoliate.

Mode of spread and survival The pathogen spreads through rain splash and survives in the infested seeds Epidemiology Poor drainage and heavy rain encourage the disease development Management Use disease free se

pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Dry root rot - Macrophomina phaseolina
Symptoms The lower leaves show yellowing, dropping and premature defoliation.
Numerous, minute, black "pycnidia" are seen on the hypocotyls and lower portions of the stems.
The lession coalesce and cause the branches or hole plant to dry up and die.
Mode of Spread Seed borne and air borne pycnidiospores primarily spread the disease.

pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Powdery mildew - Erysiphe polygoni
Symptoms White powdery growth appears on the upper surface of the leaves.
Mode of Spread and Survival The fungus is an obligate parasite.
Primary infection is usually by ascospores from cleistothecia , chasmothecia and secondary spread by air borne conidia and rain splashes.
Epidemiology The disease is severe, generally during late kharif and rabi season.

pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Rust - Uromyces phaseoli-typica
Symptoms Dark reddish - brown pustules (uredosori) appear on both surfaces of the leaves and the pustules may be surrounded by yellow halo.
Etiology Uredospores are globose, Unicellular, ellipsoid with echinucleate Teliospores are unicellular, globose , pedicellate chestnut brown in colour with warty papillae at top.
Mode of Spread and Survival The pathogen is an autoceious rus, long cycle rust which spreads through wind borne uredospores and survives in the infected plant debris.

pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Anthracnose -Colletotrichum lindemuthianum
Symptoms The fungus attacks young as well as old seedlings.
Small, round to oblong, brown spots appear on leaves, stem and pods.
Later Water soaked lesions appear later becoming brown and circular depressed with dark center.

pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Bacterial blight - Xanthomonas phaseoli
Symptoms Water soaked light yellow spots on lower surface of leaves.
Brown, circular to irregular and distinctly raised spots appear on the diseased leaves.
Etiology Bacteria are gram negative, enters through wounds or natural openings.

Mode of Spread and Survival The primary spread is through seed borne bacteria and it survives in the infected plants and crop residues Epidemiology Cool, rainy weather favours the disease development Management

pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Yellow mosaic -Yellow mosaic virus
Symptoms On the leaves irregular, yellow and green patches alternating each other appears.
Infected plants are stunted, mature later and produce very few flowers and pods.
The leaf size is generally not much altered, but sometimes the green areas are slightly raised and the leaves show slight puckering and reduction in size.
Vector The disease is transmitted by white fly -Bemisia tabaci Epidemiology Summer temperature (30-350 C) favours multiplication of vectors and the disease spread.

pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Leaf crinkle - Leaf crinkle virus
Symptoms Enlargement in size followed by crinkled surfaces of laminae were the characteristics symptoms of the affected trifoliates.
The affected plants are stunted, appear bushy, remain green and do not die till harvest.
In severe infection, all the leaves are curved downwards.
Vector The insect vectors white fly -- Bemisia tabaci and Aphid - Aphis craccivora and A.gossypii transmit the disease Epidemiology High temperature during summer period favours the disease spread.

pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Powdery mildew - Levillula taurica
Symptoms Powdery patches on the lower surface corresponding yellow patches on upper surface.
Conidia single celled and clavate.Clesitothecia are black globose with mycelial appendages and each ascus contain 3-5 ascospores.

pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Wilt - Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. udum

The fungus survives upto 2.5 years in red soil and 3 years in black soil.

pat301.t: Sterility mosaic - Red gram sterility mosaic virus
pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Sterility mosaic - Red gram sterility mosaic virus
The disease causes upto 95 per cent yield loss when the plants were infected early Symptoms The disease usually produces three types of symptoms.
Initially yellow patches intermingle with green colour of leaves.
In severe case, leaves become smaller and cluster near tip because of shortened inter nodes.
It is characterized by green islands surrounded by a chlorotic halo on leaf lets, symptoms tend to disappear as the plants mature.

pat301.t: Leaf curl - Tomato spotted wilt virus [TSWV]
pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Leaf curl - Tomato spotted wilt virus [TSWV]
Symptoms The infection starts as chlorosis of lateral veins near the leaf margins and margins slowly curl downwards.
The infected leaves are brittle and plants produce a few small and malformed pods.
Vector The disease is transmitted by Thrips viz., - Frankliniella schultzi, Thrips tabaci and Scirtothrips dorsalis Epidemiology Rainy days during kharif season favour high incidence of disease.
Management Rogue out infected plants up to 30 DAS and remove the weed host.

pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Downy mildew - Peronospora manshrica
Symptoms: Downy mildew of soybean is characterized in its early stages by indefinite yellowish green areas on the upper surface of the leaves.
As the disease progresses, those areas become grayish brown or dark brown and have yellowish green margins.
Mode of spread and survival: The spores produced on the mould growth on the leaves spread the disease from plant to plant.
Secondary spread is through air borne sporangia formed on infected leaves.

pat301.t: Soybean mosaic - Soybean mosaic virus or Soja virus I
pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Soybean mosaic - Soybean mosaic virus or Soja virus I
Symptoms: Plants infected early are stunted with shortened petioles and internodes.
Leaves are small, misshaped, puckered and occasionally with dark green enations along the veins.
Affected leaflets are generally asymmetric and curl downward at the margin.
Seedlings from infected seeds are spindly with unifoliate leaves, curled longitudinally downward and rugose or crinkled.

pat301.t: Cowpea aphid borne mosaic - Cow pea aphid borne mosaic virus
pat301.sub: Diseases of RED GRAM / PIEGON PEA
s: Cowpea aphid borne mosaic - Cow pea aphid borne mosaic virus
Symptoms The disease affected plants are stunted and the leaves show variable amounts of dark green vein banding, leaf distortion and blistering.
The infected plants produce few pods, which are small and distorted.
Transmission The disease is transmitted by insect vector aphid's viz., Aphis craccivora, A.
The virus is also seed borne and seed borne infection up to 3 per cent may be noticed.
BLAST - Pyricularia grisea
Symptoms The pathogen attacks the crop from seedling stage to the time of grain formation.
Characteristic spindle-shaped spots with yellow margin and grayish green center can be seen.
The fungus, when infects the stem causes blackening of the nodal region.
When the neck region is affected the tissues weaken and the heads droop.

pat301.t: SEEDLING BLIGHT OR LEAF BLIGHT - Helmithosporium nodulosum
s: SEEDLING BLIGHT OR LEAF BLIGHT - Helmithosporium nodulosum
Symptoms Affected young leaves show minute, light brown oval spots.
In mature plants oblong and dark brown spots are formed.
The infected spikes turn brown and are often over grown by the sooty growth of the fungus.

pat301.t: WILT OR FOOT ROT - Sclerotium rolfsii
s: WILT OR FOOT ROT - Sclerotium rolfsii
Symptoms The fungus attacks basal stem portion, leaf sheath and culm.
The infected portion becomes soft and dark brown in colour.
Later, small spherical, dark coloured sclerotia are formed in the affected areas.

Mode of spread The pathogen spreads through irrigation water and farm implements Survival The pathogen survives in the soil as soil borne sclerotia Management Crop rotation with non-host plant Spot drenching wi

pat301.t: DOWNY MILDEW / GREEN EAR / CRAZY TOP - Sclerospora macrospora
s: DOWNY MILDEW / GREEN EAR / CRAZY TOP - Sclerospora macrospora
Symptoms The infected plants produce shortened internodes and show bushy/ bunchy appearance.
Finally the abnormal spikelet produced gives a brush-like appearance.
Mode of spread The primary infection takes place from the oospores present in the soil and infested seeds.
Survival The pathogen survives in the collateral hosts and infected seeds Epidemiology Cool weather favour the disease development Management Crop rotation Roguing out the affected plants
SMUT - Melanopsichium eleusinis
Symptoms The smut fungus attacks only a few grains in an ear head.
These are converted in to enlarged globose sacs, greenish at first but later turn dirty black and 5 to 15 mm in diameter.

Mode of spread and survival The fungus spreads through air borne conidia and survives in the soil and infected spikelets Epidemiology Low temperature and high humidity favour the disease development Management
MOTTLE STREAK AND STREAK VIRUS
Symptoms The affected plants are stunted, pale green in colour.
Early infection leads to reduction of tillers and grain formation.
chinai transmit the disease Management Rogue out the infected plant Spray methyl demeton or monocrotophos 500 ml/ha at 20 days interval.

pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Blast / Rotten neck - Pyricularia grisea
The disease was first recorded in China in 1637.In India the occurrence of blast disease was first recorded from Tanjore district of Tamil Nadu in 1918.
The causal organism was first detected by Cavara in 1891 from Italy.
Symptoms The fungus attacks the crop at all stages from seedlings in nursery to heading in mainfield.
The typical symptoms appear on leaves, nodes and even the glumes are also attacked.

pat301.t: Brown spot or Sesame leaf spot - Helminthosporium oryzae/ Bipolaris oryzae
pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Brown spot or Sesame leaf spot - Helminthosporium oryzae/ Bipolaris oryzae
In India, this disease is the principal cause of Bengal famine of 1942-43.
The first report of the disease in India was made by Sundararaman from Madras in 1919.
Symptoms The fungus attacks the crop from seedling in nursery to milk stage in main field.
The perfect stage of the fungus is Cochliobolus miyabeanus and produce toxin Cochliobolin.

pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Sheath blight - Rhizoctonia solani
Symptoms The fungus affects the crop from tillering to heading stage.
Initial symptoms are noticed on leaf sheaths near water level.
The infected areas just above the water level (Collar region) are greenish grey, oval, and become grayish white with brown irregular margin on the leaf sheath.
In the advanced stages brown colour sclerotia (Irregular shaped) are formed in the infected tissues.

pat301.t: Sheath rot - Sarocladium oryzae and Sarocladium attenatum
pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Sheath rot - Sarocladium oryzae and Sarocladium attenatum
Symptoms The disease affects the boot leaf covering the panicle.
Conidia are hyaline, smooth, single celled and cylindrical in shape.
Survival and Mode of spread The pathogen survives in the infested seeds and spreads through air borne conidia.
Epidemiology Closer planting, high humidity, a temperature range of 20o - 28oC favours the disease development.

pat301.t: The disease affects the boot leaf covering the panicle or the upper most leaf sheath
pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: The disease affects the boot leaf covering the panicle or the upper most leaf sheath
Affects the crop at the collar region or the base of the plants at the water surface 2.
The disease affects the boot leaf covering the panicle or the upper most leaf sheath Affects the crop at the collar region or the base of the plants at the water surface

pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Stem rot - Sclerotium oryzae
Symptoms Stem rot infection is seen on the rice crop during early heading and grain filling stage.
Finally the infected leaf sheath rots and sclerotia are formed in the host tissues.
Mode of spread The pathogen spreads through irrigation water.
Survival The pathogen survives as soil borne sclerotia in the infected stubbles and straw Epidemiology Heavy application of nitrogen fertilizers favours the disease development.

pat301.t: Foot rot or Bakanae disease - Fusarium moniliforme
pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Foot rot or Bakanae disease - Fusarium moniliforme
In Greek "Bakane" means foolish, hence it is a foolish disease.
Symptoms The infested seedlings produce tall, lanky tillers (Bakanae) much taller than healthy seedlings and forms flower earlier than the healthy ones.
Above the ground level, adventitious roots are produced from the nodes.
Excessive elongation is due to Gibberellic acid, Phytotoxin and Fusaric acid.

pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: False smut - Ustilaginoidea virens
It is also called as Green smut or Lakshmi disease as the farmers believe that the lakshmi disease affected fields normally results in a bumper harvest.
Symptoms The disease appears on the ears and converts individual grains in to orange spore balls of velvety appearance which are small at first and more than twice the diameter of normal grain.
The infected ovaries are transformed in to large, velvety green masses (Pseudomorph).
Etiology Chlamydospores are formed on the spore balls, they are spherical to elliptical, waxy and olivaceous.

pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Udbatta disease - Ephelis oryzae
Symptoms The affected panicle emerges from the leaf sheath as a slender dirty grey coloured, cylindrical spike, rod like hard structures.
They very much resemble as "udbatta'' hence the name is given as udbatta disease.
Mode of spread and Survival The pathogen is externally seed borne and survives in the infested seeds.
Epidemiology A soil temperature of around 280 C and abundant soil moisture favour the disease.

pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Grain discolouration -Fungal complex disease
Symptoms Dark brown to black spots appear on the grains.
Many fungi are found involved in the disease depending on the locality.
Mode of spread and Survival The pathogens spreads through air borne conidia and survives in the infected plant debris, grains and collateral hosts.
Epidemiology High humidity and cloudy weather favour the disease development.

pat301.t: Bacterial leaf blight - Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae
pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Bacterial leaf blight - Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae
A severe outbreak of the disease occurred in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh in 1963.
In the tropics the disease is usually referred as bacterial blight as it often kills entire young seedlings .
Under humid condition, creamy white bacterial ooze characteristics of the disease can also be observed.
''kresek'' or wilt phase Wilt syndrome known as Kresek is seen in seedlings within 3-4 weeks after transplanting of the crop.

pat301.t: Bacterial leaf streak - Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola
pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Bacterial leaf streak - Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola
Symptoms The infected leaves shows fine translucent streaks on the veins and the lesions enlarge lengthwise and turn brown.
Etiology The organism is short rod, about 1.2μ x 0.3 to 0.5μ, and gram negative.
Mode of spread The bacterium spreads through air and wind splashed rains.
Survival The bacterium survives in the infested seeds Epidemiology Rain splash and irrigation water favour the disease development.

pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Tungro - Rice tungro virus [RTV]
Symptoms The infected plants show yellow to orange discolouration of leaves and rusty blotches spreading downwards from the leaf tip.
The infected plants produce few spikelets and panicles are small with discoloured grains.
Yellow discoloration is commonly seen in "Japonica" varieties, while "Indica" varieties show orange discoloration.
Vector The disease is spread through green leaf hopper Nephotettix virescens and N.

pat301.t: Grassy stunt - Rice grassy stunt virus
pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Grassy stunt - Rice grassy stunt virus
Symptoms Infected plants are stunted and produce excess tillers and have erect growth habit.
Leaves are short, narrow, pale green / pale yellow and have numerous rusty brown spots of various shapes.
Vector The disease is spread by brown plant hopper (Nilaparvata lugens) in a persistent manner.
Management Rogueing and Field sanitation Use systemic insecticides to control the vector Grow resistant varieties like IR-28, IR-29, IR-30, IR-32, IR-34.

pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Dwarf - Rice dwarf virus
Symptoms The infected plants show marked stunted growth with chlorotic or whitish specks on the leaves.
The number of tillers may be reduced with retarded root growth.

Vector Leaf hopper Nephotettix nigropictus and Recilia dorsalis Also weeds like Echinochloa crusgalli harbour the pathogen during off-seasons Management Rogueing and Field sanitation to destroy the weed host Sp

pat301.sub: LECTURE- 1- DISEASES OF RICE- Oryza sativa
s: Yellow dwarf - Phytoplasma disease
Symptoms The infected plants are stunted and have yellowish green to whitish green leaves with excessive tillering and leaves become soft and droop slightly.
nigropictus transmit the disease Management Deep ploughing in summer and burning the stubbles.
CHARCOAL ROT-Macrophomina phaseolina
Symptoms The fungus invades through the roots and the lower stem of the infected plants become soft and weak resulting in lodging and poor grain filling.
When infected stem is split open, vascular fibres could be seen disintegrated and black sclerotia can be seen heavily coated in the tissues and hence the name charcoal rot.
Mode of spread The pathogen spreads through transfer of infested soil by agricultural implements and irrigation water.
Survival The pathogen survives as sclerotia in soil and plant debris Epidemiology Drought stress makes the plant weak and susceptible.

pat301.t: DOWNY MILDEW OR LEAF SHREADING - Perenosclerospora sorghi
s: DOWNY MILDEW OR LEAF SHREADING - Perenosclerospora sorghi
Symptoms Whitish soft downy growth can be seen on the lower surface of the leaves with corresponding yellowing on the upper surface of the leaves.
After the oospore formation in the vascular bundle, leaf blade tear in to stripes with the midrib remaining intact producing the characteristic "leaf shredding" symptom.
Mode of spread Oospores form the primary inoculum and the air borne sporangia forms the secondary inoculum.
Survival The pathogen survives as oospores in soil for 3-4 years and survives as mycelium in seeds.
RUST - Puccinia purpurea
Symptoms Rust is a severe disease of sorghum capable of infecting the leaves at all stages of the crop growth when the environment is favorable.
The reddish brown sori are minute, round or elliptical and 1-2 mm in diameter.
Mode of spread and Survival Uredospores are spread by air.
Pycnial and aecial stages survive on the alternate host Oxalis corniculata) Epidemiology Generally rainy weather and low temperatures favour the disease development.

pat301.t: GRAIN SMUT / KERNAL SMUT / COVERED SMUT - Sporisorium sorghi
s: GRAIN SMUT / KERNAL SMUT / COVERED SMUT - Sporisorium sorghi
Symptoms The disease appears only at the time of grain formation.
The individual grains are replaced by smut sori which are oval / conical shaped and cream to light brown in colournd 5-15mm long nd 3-5 mm broad.
These are covered by cream to light brown skin (Peridium) which remains unbroken upto threshing.
The fungus is present in the form of sorus, which has a tough wall and a long, hard, central tissue called columellum.
LOOSE SMUT - Sporisorium cruenta
Symptoms The affected plants are stunted, produce thinner stalks.
All the spikelets of the infected ears are malformed and hypertrophied.
Mode of spread and Survival The fungus is externally seed borne and soil borne.
Epidemiology Low temperature, dry soil moisture and high humidity encourages the disease.The optimum time for spore germination is 30⁰C.
LONG SMUT - Tolyposporium ehrenbergii
Symptoms Usually a few smut sori appear and scattered on earhead.
The sorus is covered by a whitish to dull yellow, fairly thick membrane (Peridium) and is much longer than those of the other two smuts.
The sori are cylindrical, elongated and creamy brown coloured.
Etiology The spores are firmly united into balls and measure 12-16 µm Mode of spread and Survival The pathogen spreads through air borne smut spores/sporidia.
HEAD SMUT - Sporisorium reiliana
Symptoms The disease appears only at the time of flowering.
The head is partially or fully replaced by a large sorus when still in the boot leaf.
The galls are first covered by a whitish grey membrane in the boot leaf, later turn to brown/ black coloured masses.
Mode of spread and Survival The pathogen is soil borne and survives in soil for two years.
ERGOT/SUGARY DISEASE - Sphacelia sorghi (Claviceps sorghi)
Symptoms The disease occurs only at the time of flowering.
The honey dew is colonized by saprophytic fungi giving a blackened appearance.
Mode of spread and Survival The pathogen spreads through air borne conidia and insects.
The honey dew attracts the insects and ants which help in spreading the disease.
Leaf blight - Helminthosporium turcicum
Symptoms In the initial stage, small, narrow, elongated spots appear on the leaf.
On older plants, the typical symptoms are long elliptical necrotic lesions, straw coloured in the center with dark margins.
Mode of spread and Survival The pathogen spreads through infested seed and the secondary spread is through the air borne conidia.
Epidemiology Cool moist weather, high humidity and rainfall encourage the disease development.
Rectangular leaf spot - Cercospora sorghi
Small rectangular leaf spots of dark brown colour, bounded by veins with irregular borders appear on both the surface of the leaves.
Mode of spread and Survival The pathogen spreads through air borne conidia and survives in the infected plant debris and collateral hosts.
Epidemiology Cool moist weather, high humidity (above 90 %) and rainfall favour the disease development.
Management Spray ziram 0.2% or dusting sulphur @ 25Kg/ha

pat301.t: Anthracnose and red rot - Colletotrichum graminicola
s: Anthracnose and red rot - Colletotrichum graminicola
Symptoms The pathogen causes both leaf spot and stalk rot diseases.
The disease appears as small red coloured spots on both surfaces of the leaf.
Mode of spread and Survival The primary infection is through infested seeds and secondary spread is through air borne conidia.
The pathogen survives in the infected plant debris and collateral hosts.

pat301.t: Witch weed - Striga asiatica and Striga densiflora
s: Witch weed - Striga asiatica and Striga densiflora
Symptoms Striga is a small plant with bright green leaves, grows upto a height of 15-30 cm.
Mode of spread and survival The seeds are spread by wind, water and farm tools/machinery contaminated with the infested soil.
The seeds of the parasite are found viable for many years in the soil.
Management Regular weeding and inter cultural operations during early stage of parasite growth Spraying with sodium salt of 2,4-D 80% at 450g/500 lit of water kills the parasite.

OBJECTIVES AND SCOPE OF THE BREEDING Plant breeding is an art and science, which tells us ways and means to change the genetic architecture of plants so as to attain a particular objective.
The objectives may be a) Crop Improvement b) Improved agronomic characters c) Resistance against biotic and abiotic stress.
Majority of our breeding programmes aim at increased yield.
Section 1 (contd. 2)
The classical examples are utilization of Dee Gee Woo Gen in rice and Norin - 10 in wheat.
Identification and utilization of male sterility is another example.
Improving the quality is another aim in crop improvement.
For example, - Rice it may be milling, cooking quality, aroma and grain colour.
- In wheat, milling and baking quality and gluten content.
Section 1 (contd. 3)
- Protein content and improving sulphur containing amino acids in pulses.
Elimination of toxic substance is yet another aim of crop improvement.
- Lathyrogen content in Lathyrus sativus (βN oxalyamine alanine BOAA) - Erucic acid in Brassicas - Cucurbitacin in cucurbits.
Improved agronomic characters: - Production of more tillers - E.g.
- Elimination of season bound characters - Redgram, Sorghum - Reducing the plant height to prevent lodging - Rice.
Section 1 (contd. 4)
- Elimination or introduction of dormancy - Potato, Groundnut.
Biotic stress: Pests and diseases, Evolving resistant varieties reduce cost of cultivation, environmental pollution and saving beneficial insects.
Soil factors and edaphic factors som e times poses severe problems.
Breeding resistant varieties is th e easy way to co mbat abiotic stress.

There are two ways by which yield improvement is possible.
Enhancing the productivity of crops This can be done a) by the proper m anagement of soil and crops involving suitable agronomic practices and harvesting physical resources.
by using high potential crop varieties crea ted by appropriate genetic m anipulation of crop plants.

Stabilizing the productivity achieved This is done by using crop varieties that are bred especially for wide adaptation or for specific crop zones to offset the ill effects of unfavourable environmental cond it
Plant breeding, the past, present and future scopes Indian agriculture remained stagnant particularly during early sixties.
Section 1 (contd. 6)
Long spells of severe drought and serious out break of disease in some parts of the country led som e futurologists to state that a possible doom in India by the end of the decade.
However we achieved a break through in crops such as Rice, wheat, Pearl millet, Jowar and Maize.
The indica x japonica cross derivative ADT 27 (GEB 24 x Norin 10) is the first high yielding rice of Tamil Nadu.
The identification of Dee Gee Woo Gen and release of Wonder rice IR 8 (peta x DGWG) changed th e scenario from poverty to problem of plenty.

Like wise identification of dwarfing gene in Japanese wheat variety Norin - 10 by Borlaug and breeding of Mexican dwarf wheat varieties led to th e release of wheat varieties life Kalyan sona in India.

Agriculture is the deliberate planting and harvesting of plants and herding animals.
This human invention has, and continues to, impact on society and the environment.
Plant breeding is a branch of agriculture that focuses on manipulating plant heredity to develop new and improved plant types for use by society.
What is plant breeding? Plant breeding is a deliberate effort by humans to nudge nature , with respect to the heredity of plants, to an advantage.
PBG Notes (contd. 2)
The professionals who conduct this task are called plant breeders.
Consequently, the term "plant breeding" is often used synonymously with "plant improvement" in modern society.
The goals of plant breeding are focused and purposeful Breeding is hence about manipulating plant attributes, structure, and composition, to make them more useful to humans.
Why breed plants? The reasons for manipulating plant attributes or performance change according to the needs of society.
Plants provide food, feed, fiber, pharmaceuticals, and shelter for humans.
PBG Notes (contd. 3)
Furthermore, plants are used for aesthetic and other functional purposes in the landscape and indoors.
Goals of plant breeding  The plant breeder uses various technologies and methodologies to achieve targeted and directional changes in the nature of plants.
 Breeders aim to make the crop producer's job easier and more effective in various ways.
 Breeders may also develop high-yielding varieties (or cultivars) so the farmer can produce more for the market to meet consumer demands while improving his or her income.
Vengadessan Lecture 1  They may modify plant structure so it can resist lodging and thereby facilitate mechanical harvesting.
PBG Notes (contd. 4)
 They may develop plants that resist pests so the farmer does not have to apply pesticides or can apply smaller amounts of these chemicals.
Not applying pesticides in crop production means less environmental pollution from agricultural sources.
 When breeders think of consumers, they may, for example, develop foods with higher nutritional value and that are more flavorful.
 Plant breeders may also target traits of industrial value.

Addressing world food, feed, and nutritional needs  Food is the most basic of human needs.
 Plants are the primary producers in the ecosystem (a community of living organisms including all the non-living factors in the environment).
 Plant breeding is needed to enhance the value of food crops, by improving their yield and the nutritional quality of their products, for healthy living of humans.

 Certain plant foods are deficient in certain essential nutrients to the extent that where these foods constitute the bulk of a staple diet, diseases associated with nutritional deficiency are often common.
