Lecture notes SAC301-18-34
Root interception Root interception occurs when a nutrient comes into physical contact with the root surface.
As a general rule, the occurrence of root interception increases as the root surface area and mass increases, thus enabling the plant to explore a greater amount of soil.
Root interception may be enhanced by mycorrhizal fungi, which colonize roots and increases root exploration into the soil.
Root interception is responsible for an appreciable amount of calcium uptake, and some amounts of magnesium, zinc and manganese.
The CEC of roots for monocots is 10 - 30 meq/100 g and takes up monovalent cations more readily and that of Dicots is 40 - 100 meq/100 g and takes up divalent cations more readily.
Lecture notes SAC301-18-34 (contd. 2)
The quantity of nutrients intercepted by roots depends on the soil concentration of nutrients and volume of soil displaced by root system Factors affecting root interception a.

Root growth is necessary for all three mechanisms of nutrient supply, but absolutely essential for root interception to occur Mass flow Mass flow occurs when nutrients are transported to the surface of roots by
The rate of water flow governs the amount of nutrients that are transported to the root surface.
Most of the nitrogen, calcium, magnesium, sulfur, copper, boron, manganese and molybdenum move to the root by mass flow.
Solution concentration of nutrient Nutrients supplied primarily by mass flow are considered mobile nutrients.
Lecture notes SAC301-18-34 (contd. 3)
Root density much less critical for nutrient supply by mass flow than for root interception and diffusion Diffusion: Diffusion is the movement of a particular nutrient along a concentration gradient.
When there is a difference in concentration of a particular nutrient within the soil solution, the nutrient will move from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
As the sugar dissolves, it moves through parts of the water with lower sugar concentration until it is evenly distributed, or uniformly concentrated.
Diffusion delivers appreciable amounts of phosphorus, potassium, zinc , and iron to the root surface.
Diffusion is a relatively slow process compared to the mass flow of nutrients with water movement toward the root.
Lecture notes SAC301-18-34 (contd. 4)
Nutrients supplied primarily by diffusion are considered immobile nutrients e.g.

Effective diffusion coefficient Effective diffusion coefficient D e = Dw * q * (1/T) * (1/b) where Dw = diffusion coefficient in water q = volumetric soil water content T = tortuosity factor b = soil buffering
Nutrients can be removed by adsorption as they move through soil, reducing diffusion rate c.
Size and density of plant root systems is very important for nutrients supplied by diffusion c.
Has implications for fertilizer placement Movement of ions into the root Mineral nutrients absorbed from the root has to be carried to the xylem.
Lecture notes SAC301-18-34 (contd. 5)
This transport follows two pathways namely apoplastic and symplastic pathways.
In Apoplastic pathway, mineral nutrients along with water moves from cell to cell through spaces between cell wall by diffusion.
The ions, which enter the cell wall of the epidermis move across cell wall of cortex, cytoplasm of endodermis, cell walls of pericycle and finally reach the xylem.
In Symplastic pathway, mineral nutrients entering the cytoplasm of the epidermis move across the cytoplasm of the cortex, endodermis of pericycle through plasmodesmata and finally reach the xylem.
Translocation of solutes Mineral nutrients absorbed by the roots are translocated through the xylem vessel.
Lecture notes SAC301-18-34 (contd. 6)
Mineral salts dissolved in water moves up along the xylem vessel to be transported to all the parts of the plant body.
As water is continuously lost by transpiration on the upper surfaces of the plant, it creates a transpirational pull, by which water along with mineral salts is pulled up along the xylem vessel.
Absorption of mineral nutrients by plants is through active and passive absorption.
Active absorption is achieved only by an input of energy.
Metabolic energy helps in the absorption of mineral salts.

Mechanism of Nutrient transport to plants There are sixteen nutrients that are essential for plant growth and development.
After taken in by the roots, the nutrients move into the plant and are used for various functions and processes.
Nutrient absorption and utilization is not a simplistic process.
SAC 301 - After midsem (contd. 2)
The discussion that follows will foc us on movement to the root.
Plants don't necessarily grow in search of plant nutrients.
Nutrients must get to the plant root to be absorbed by the large number of root hairs.
Root hairs live in association with a diverse group of fungi called mycorrhizae which aid the movement of a nutrient from outside to inside of the root itself.
There's general agreement among plant physiologists that there are three mechanisms by which nutrients reach the surface of the root hairs.
SAC 301 - After midsem (contd. 3)
These are: 1) root interception, 2) mass flow, and 3) diffusion.
Root Interception Soil particles of various sizes (sand, silt, clay) with organic matter acting as a glue are formed into soil aggregates of various shapes and sizes.
However, in growth and development, plant roots come in contact with a very limited of soil surface within the aggregates -about 1% to 2%.
Roots usually grow around the soil aggregates and don't grow into them.
Thus most plant roots don't contact a large percentage of the very extensive surface of the soil aggregates.
SAC 301 - After midsem (contd. 4)
Therefore, the process of roots making direct contact with soil aggregates (root interception), although important, can't be a major mechanism for nutrients to reach the surface of the root.
Mass Flow Driven by the physiological process of transpiration (water loss through the leaves), water moves from the soil pores into the plant root.
The soil water contains three negatively charged ions of nitrogen (nitrate), sulfur (sulfate) and boron (borate).
Likewise, all of the negatively charged ions in this water will not be used by plants.
Some of the water and the nutrients contained in this water moves below the root zone.
SAC 301 - After midsem (contd. 5)
Many of the concerns about environmental quality revolve around leaching.

By monitoring nutrients in water in tile lines and water moving through sandy soils, the Discovery Farms -Minnesota initiative is measuring the amount of water and, especially nitrogen, that moves below the roo
The quantity of these three nutrients that reach the root surface via mass flow is not a constant value.
There are several management practices that affect water use by plants as well as the amount of nitrate, sulfate, and borate in this water.

Diffusion For the essential nutrients that have a positive electrical charge when dissolved in the soil water, the major mechanism of nutrient movement to the root surface is the very slow process of diffusion.
SAC 301 - After midsem (contd. 6)
The positively charged nutrients are potassium (K+), calcium (Ca++), magnesium (Mg++) and the micronutrients except for boron.
These positively charged nutrients are associated with the clay component of the soil aggregates.
Using a chemistry definition , diffusion is the movement of a nutrient ion from an area of high concentration to an area of lower concentration.
In soil system, the surface of the root is usually considered to be the area of lower concentration.
The surface of the clays in the soil aggregates is thought to be the area of high concentration.

Agricultural Credit System in India
Farmers get external financial assistance from two sources namely, i) non- institutional or unorganized agencies, and ii) institutional or organized agencies.
It is a fact that agriculture has been financed by non-institutional agencies for a long time and institutional agencies were started functioning only during the early part of twentieth century.

aec302.t: Non-Institutional Sources of Finance in India
s: Non-Institutional Sources of Finance in India
Non-institutional sources include money lenders, land lords, traders, commission agents, friends and relatives.
Money Lenders There are two types of money lenders in rural areas namely agricultural money lenders and professional money lender.
Agricultural money lender's main occupation is farming and money lending is secondary one.
Although the reliance on money lender by rural poor declined over the years, the credit disbursed by money lenders still forms a major portion of the total credit obtained by the farmers.
Disadvantages /Unfair Practices of Money Lenders
Often small farmers are forced to sell out their lands to these land lords and they become land less labourers and bonded labourers.
Traders and Commission Agents They are functioning either to get regular supply of products for their trade or to have a control over the provision of credit by other creditors.
Though the rate of interest charged by them is not as high as charged by the money lenders, they charge more in the form of concessions and service changes.
Since all farmers are living under similar conditions, they cannot lend large sums as loans.
Need for Institutional Credit Agencies

Although, the private agencies satisfied some of the criteria of a good system of credit, their loan were not related to production purposes, they never cared for the end use of the loan extended and the loan i
However, institutions adopt a productive and purpose oriented credit policy while providing credit.
So this policy made the institutions to discourage the provision of credit to consumption purpose.
But it is evident that the need for consumption loan in rural households continues to persist.
Institutional Credit Agencies

As compared to the quantum of credit requirement and the capacity of institutions to meet these credit demands under multi-agency system, it is impossible to completely wipe out the private agencies from the ru
.The repayment plan is convenient, i.e., repayment in equal annual installments.
Demerits 1) Quantum of loan is determined on the basis of value of security offered, by which, large farmers receive more credit than small and marginal farmers.
) As these loans are not production oriented, they do not satisfy the standard needed for sound system of form credit.
Extent of Rural Indebtedness
Causes of Rural indebtedness: Rural indebtedness is caused mostly by economic and social factors.
Moreover, farmers are also often affected by flood, drought etc.
Just as poverty forces him to borrow, it is this poverty again forces him to have so little far repaying his debt.
Consequently, the farm productivity is extremely low and it does not allow them to get out of indebtedness.
Consequences of Rural Indebtedness
Incentive to efficient farming and increase of agricultural production is curtailed.
Farmers mortgage their properties to the money lenders and ultimately lose it to the latter.
Farmer is hit hard through the adverse terms of trade, i.e., he has low bargaining power as he has to sell his produces to the money lender from whom he has borrowed.
Because of deprivation of land, the cultivators not only suffer economically but also they are pushed down in the social hierarchy.
Remedies for Rural Indebtedness
The problem of rural indebtedness has to be tackled in two ways: i) the burden of present indebtedness should be reduced, and ii) indebtedness in future should be controlled.

Reducing the Burden of Present Indebtedness Since the major cause of continued indebtedness of rural poor is the malpractices adopted by money lenders, many states have taken steps like prescribing maximum rate
Many states enacted laws according to which the borrower cannot be asked to pay more than twice the loan amount taken by him.
In many states, Debt Conciliation Boards were set up and these boards could review the debt repaying capacity of the borrower and reduce the debt compulsorily if it found excessive.

Rabi season and crop planning
Rabi crops are sown after the monsoon, generally from October to November, and harvested in spring.
The main rabi crops are wheat, chickpea, mustard, barley, lentil and, in the south, rice and pulses.
The season is planned around the moisture already stored in the soil and the water available for irrigation.
Choosing a variety of the right duration is the first decision, because the crop must finish before the heat sets in.
Land preparation for rabi crops
Prepare a fine, well-levelled seedbed so that the seed is placed at a uniform depth and germinates evenly.
In heavy soils, work the land when it is at the right moisture; working it wet destroys structure and working it dry makes clods.
Levelling matters even more in the rabi season, because a level field irrigates uniformly with less water.
Retain the moisture in the seed zone by closing the soil after the final harrowing.
Sowing on residual moisture
Much of the rabi crop is sown on the moisture stored from the previous monsoon, so timing is critical.
Sow as soon as the soil reaches the right moisture; delay means the seed zone dries and germination fails.
Where the stored moisture is not enough, give a pre-sowing irrigation and sow at the right moisture after it.
Place the seed at the recommended depth: too deep delays emergence and too shallow leaves it to dry.
Fertilizer management in rabi crops
Apply the full dose of phosphorus and potassium and a part of the nitrogen as a basal dose at sowing.
Top dress the remaining nitrogen in one or two splits, timed with irrigation.
Nitrogen applied to dry soil is wasted, so fertilizer should go on when the soil has moisture.
In the cooler rabi season the crop grows slower, so the first top dressing is usually given after the first irrigation.
Irrigation scheduling in rabi
With little rain in the season, the rabi crop depends on irrigation at the correct stages.
In wheat the crown root stage, about three weeks after sowing, is the single most critical irrigation.
Irrigate when the available soil moisture in the root zone falls to the level at which the crop begins to suffer.
Light soils need smaller, more frequent irrigations than heavy soils, which hold water longer.
Weed management in rabi crops
Weeds compete most strongly in the first few weeks, so early control gives the largest return.
Both mechanical weeding and recommended herbicides are used, depending on the crop and the weed flora.
In wheat, a broadleaf herbicide applied at the right stage controls the common weeds without hurting the crop.
A dense, well-fed crop canopy shades the ground and by itself suppresses later weed growth.

agr303.t: Pest and disease management in rabi
s: Pest and disease management in rabi
Aphids build up on wheat and mustard in the cool season and must be watched on the ears and pods.
Pulses in this season face pod borers and pod fly, which are managed by monitoring and need-based spraying.
Rusts appear on wheat in cool, moist spells, so scout the lower leaves as the crop grows.
Spray only when the pest or disease crosses the threshold, and observe the waiting period before harvest.
Growth observations and yield estimation
Record plant height, tiller or branch number and the stage of the crop at fixed intervals.
Tag representative plants and follow the same ones through the season so that the record is comparable.
Estimate yield from the yield components measured in quadrats, such as ears per square metre and grains per ear.
Compare the estimate with the actual threshed produce, and note the reasons for any gap.
Harvest, threshing and storage
Harvest at the correct maturity; early harvest gives shrivelled grain and late harvest causes shattering.
Rabi crops mature in the dry season, so the grain usually comes in at a lower moisture than in the kharif.
Thresh on a clean floor and dry the produce to the safe moisture level before it is stored or sold.
Store in a clean, dry, ventilated place and treat against storage insects as recommended.

agr303.t: Cost of cultivation and farm records
s: Cost of cultivation and farm records
Cost of cultivation covers every expense on the crop, from land preparation through to the market.
Maintain a simple record of operations, inputs and labour, because without records the cost cannot be worked out.
Gross income is the value of the produce and net income is that value minus the cost of cultivation.
The benefit-cost ratio and the net return per hectare show whether the rabi crop paid for itself.

Assembly language

Machine language
We know that a computer can understand only special signals, which are represented by 1s and 0s.
The language, which uses binary digits, is called machine language.
Writing a program in machine language is definitely very difficult.
It is not possible to memorise along string of 0s and 1s for every instruction.
Assembly language
For example ADD for addition operation, SUB for subtraction operation, etc.
It is easier to write computer programs in assembly language as compared to machine language.
It is machine dependent and programmer requires knowledge of computer architecture.
High Level Languages (HLL)
These are like English languages and are simpler to understand than the assembly language or machine language.
High level language is not understandable to the computer.
A computer program written in a high level language is to be converted into its equivalent machine language program.
Examples of high level programming languages are BASIC, C, C++, Java, etc.
Need for language processor
The programs consisting of instructions to the computer, written in assembly language or high level language are not understood by the computer.
We need language processors to convert such programs into low level language, as computer can only understand machine language.
Language processors are the system programs that translate programs written in high level language or assembly language into its equivalent machine language.

The procedures required for each of the listed procedures are accepted as measures of compost stability.
At this time the most widely used and commonly accepted methods for determining compost stability are based on respirometry.
Respirometry is the measurement of carbon dioxide evolved or oxygen consumed by microorganisms within the material, which provides an estimate of potential biological activity.
A stable compost is not biologically inert, as the presence of microorganisms is dependent upon continued availability of biodegradable organic matter.
Oxygen Uptake Rate
Although oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide generation or evolution are related, the measurements are not consistently equivalent.

Generally the measurement of oxygen consumption requires more sophistication, time and quality control, in comparison to the more simple and often more precise measurement of carbon dioxide evolution.
In comparison to the methods based on respirometry, the method is relatively simple and provides data that is easy to understand, as units of heat.

Oxygen Uptake Rate (OUR Test)
The changes in oxygen concentration with time in the air space of a closed container containing a moist compost sample of known volume and weight, at known temperature and pressure is monitored.
Samples are adjusted to 40-50 percent moisture, then samples are pre-incubated in bags placed in a constant temperature environment at 37� § C and 100 percent humidity for a minimum of 24 hours.
The sample is then added to a container that is sealed with appropriate monitoring equipment to allow measurement of oxygen consumption every minute for at least 90 minutes.
The results are calculated as oxygen uptake per unit of total sample solids (see Section 5, Definitions).
Carbon Dioxide Evolution Rate
The amount of carbon dioxide released with time in the air space of a closed container containing a moist compost sample of known volume, weight, at known temperature and pressure is monitored.
Samples are adjusted to approximately 50 percent moisture, then samples are pre-incubated in bags placed in a chamber at 37§ C and 100% humidity for 3 days.

The sample is then added to a container that is sealed 3-5 California Compost Quality Council Compost Maturity Index June 2001 www.ccqc.org with appropriate monitoring equipment to allow daily measurement of ca
The results are calculated as carbon dioxide evolved per unit of total sample solids and total biodegradable volatile solids.
Respiration Rate (Soil Control Laboratory)
The basic elements of this respiration test are similar to the other CO2 evolution rate tests with a few modifications.
Following removal of large particles (>4 mm) and inerts, the material is mixed with saturated sand (about 4:1 ratio) to adjust moisture and ensure uniform release of carbon dioxide.
After three days several sub-samples are aerated then are incubated for one hour at 37 oC and the resulting carbon dioxide concentration in the air space of the container is determined.
The results are calculated as carbon dioxide evolution per unit of volatile solids.

ens301.sub: Waste water Recycle - Constructed wetlands - Reed
s: Uses of recycled water
By providing an additional source of water, water recycling can help us find ways to decrease the diversion of water from sensitive ecosystems.
Other benefits include decreasing wastewater discharges and reducing and preventing pollution.
Plants, wildlife, and fish depend on sufficient water flows to their habitats to live and reproduce.
The lack of adequate flow, as a result of diversion for agricultural, urban, and industrial purposes, can cause deterioration of water quality and ecosystem health.

ens301.t: Water recycling can reduce and prevent pollution
ens301.sub: Waste water Recycle - Constructed wetlands - Reed
s: Water recycling can reduce and prevent pollution
When pollutant discharges to oceans, rivers, and other water bodies are curtailed, the pollutant loadings to these bodies are decreased.
Moreover, in some cases, substances that can be pollutants when discharged to a body of water can be beneficially reused for irrigation.
For example, recycled water may contain higher levels of nutrients, such as nitrogen, than potable water.

ens301.sub: Waste water Recycle - Constructed wetlands - Reed
s: Recycling water can save energy
As the demand for water grows, more water is extracted, treated, and transported sometimes over great distances which can require a lot of energy.
If the local source of water is ground water, the level of ground water becomes lower as more water is removed and this increases the energy required to pump the water to the surface.
Recycling water on site or nearby reduces the energy needed to move water longer distances or pump water from deep within an aquifer.
Tailoring water quality to a specific water use also reduces the energy needed to treat water.

It also indirectly widens the ambit of permitted activities by inserting the 'wise use' principle, giving powers to state-level wetland authorities to decide what can be allowed in larger interest.
Domestic Wastewater

Although domestic wastewater originates from domestic household activities, it can also include water that is discharged from commercial and business buildings and institutions, along with ground water.
Water that collects from a storm can also be present in domestic wastewater.
The source of domestic wastewater typically consists of liquid discharge from sanitary facilities, bathing, laundry and cooking.
This type of water can be treated due to its characteristics.
Industrial Wastewater
Industrial wastewater, which originates from the manufacturing process, can be more difficult to treat due to the examination that must take place at an industry- based level.
Industrial sources of wastewater contain contaminants such as oils, pharmaceuticals, pesticides, silt, chemicals and other by products.
Different types of water pollutants can be classified in to following major categories:
Synthetic Organic Compounds
Through various manmade activities such as production of these compounds, spillage during transportation, and their uses in different applications.
These include synthetic pesticides, synthetic detergents, food additives, pharmaceuticals, insecticides, paints, synthetic fibers, plastics, solvents and volatile organic compounds (VOCs).
Most of these compounds are toxic and biorefractory organics i.e., they are resistant to microbial degradation.
Pathogens The pathogenic microorganisms enter in to water body through sewage discharge as a major source or through the wastewater from industries like slaughterhouses.
Suspended Solids And Sediments
These comprise of silt, sand and minerals eroded from land.
These appear in the water through the surface runoff during rainy season and through municipal sewers.
This can lead to the siltation, reduces storage capacities of reservoirs.
Presence of suspended solids can block the sunlight penetration in the water, which is required for the photosynthesis by bottom vegetation.
Inorganic Pollutants
These compounds are non-biodegradable and persist in the environment.
These pollutants include mineral acids, inorganic salts, trace elements, metals, metals compounds, complexes of metals with organic compounds, cyanides, sulphates, etc.
Thermal Pollution
Discharge of hot water from thermal power plants, nuclear power plants, and industries where water is used as coolant.
As a result of hot water discharge, the temperature of water body increases.
Rise in temperature reduces the DO content of the water, affecting adversely the aquatic life.
Radioactive Pollutants
Radioactive materials originate from the following:  Mining and processing of ores,  Use in research, agriculture, medical and industrial activities, such as I131, P32, Co60, Ca45, S35, C14, etc.
 Radioactive discharge from nuclear power plants and nuclear reactors, e.g., Sr90, Cesium Cs137, Plutonium Pu248, Uranium-238, Uranium-235,  Uses and testing of nuclear weapons.
they accumulate in the bones, teeth and can cause serious disorders.
Disorders Some pollutants like sodium can cause cardiovascular diseases, while mercury and lead cause nervous disorders.
Toxic Substances
DDT is toxic material which can cause chromosomal changes.
Some of these substances like pesticides, methyl mercury etc., move into the bodies of organisms from the medium in which these organisms live which causes biomagnification.

Breeding for insect resistance
Insect resistance It is the property of a variety of a host crop due to which it is attacked by an insect pest to a significantly lower degree than other varieties of the same host.
Thus, resistance is a relative property and can be defined only in comparison to other more susceptible varieties.
Biotypes: Different strains of an insect pest differing in their ability to infest varieties of the same host species are called biotype Types of resistance a.
Host evasion: Certain crops pass through the most susceptible stage quickly or when the insect population is too small to inflict any damage b.
Mechanism of insect resistance
❖ Insect resistance is grouped into four categories: (1) Nonpreference / Antixenosis (2) Antibiosis (3) Tolerance (4) Avoidance.
❖ The first three types of resistance were recognized by Painter (1951), while the fourth, avoidance, was included subsequently.
❖ In some cases of insect resistance, non-preference, antibiosis and tolerance are simultaneously involved.
❖ Such combinations of resistance mechanisms are highly effective and are not easily overcome by the concerned insect pest.

Plant diseases are caused by a wide range of organisms such as fungi , bacteria , viruses, mycoplasma and nematodes.

Immune reaction : Host does not show the symptoms of a disease iii) Resistance reaction : Infection and establishment takes place but growth of the pathogen in the host is restricted iv).

Ideotype Breeding
✓Ideotype breeding or plant type breeding can be defined as a method of crop improvement which is used to enhance genetic yield potential through genetic manipulation of individual plant character.
✓In other words, plant characters are chosen in such a way that each character contributes towards increased economic yield.
✓In broad sense an ideotype is a biological model which is expected to perform or behave in a predictable manner within a defined environment.
✓More specifically, crop ideotype is a plant model which is expected to yield greater quantity of grains, fibre, oil or other useful product when developed as a cultivar.
Main features of Ideotype Breeding
Emphasis on Individual Trait: ◦ In ideotype breeding, emphasis is given on individual morphological and physiological trait which enhances the yield.
◦ The value of each character is specified before initiating the breeding work.
Includes Yield Enhancing Traits: ◦ Various plant characters to be included in the ideotype are identified through correlation analysis.
◦ Only those characters which exhibit positive association with yield are included in the model.

Economics: meaning and scope
Economics studies how people use scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants.
Microeconomics deals with the individual consumer, firm and market, while macroeconomics deals with the economy as a whole.
Agricultural economics applies these ideas to farming, food and the rural economy.
Its scope in agriculture runs from production decisions on the farm to prices, trade and policy.
Law of diminishing marginal utility
Utility is the satisfaction a consumer gets from a good or service.
The law of diminishing marginal utility states that as more units of a good are consumed, the satisfaction from each extra unit falls.
The equi-marginal utility principle says a consumer allocates income so that the utility per rupee is equal across all goods.
An indifference curve shows the combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same level of satisfaction.
Laws of returns in production
A production function shows the physical relationship between inputs and the output obtained.
The law of diminishing returns states that adding more of one variable input, with others fixed, eventually gives a smaller extra output.
The three stages of production are distinguished by the behaviour of the average and marginal product.
Rational producers operate in the second stage, where marginal product is falling but still positive.
National income concepts
National income is the money value of all goods and services produced by a country in a year.
Gross domestic product measures output produced within the country's borders.
Gross national product adds the income earned abroad by residents and subtracts what is paid to non-residents.
The circular flow of income shows the movement of income between households and firms through factor payments and spending.
The communication process
Communication is the process of sharing ideas, facts and feelings so that the receiver understands the message.
The basic elements are the sender, the message, the channel, the receiver and the feedback.
Effective communication is measured not by how well it is said but by how well it is understood.
In extension work, two-way communication with feedback is far more effective than simply giving information.
Barriers to communication
Communication barriers are the factors that distort or block the message between sender and receiver.
Physical barriers include distance, noise and a poor channel, and can often be removed.
Semantic barriers arise from language, jargon and words that mean different things to different people.
Psychological barriers include prejudice, lack of attention and distrust between the parties.
Listening and note taking
Listening is an active skill that requires attention, interpretation and response, unlike mere hearing.
Good listening habits include looking at the speaker, avoiding interruption and asking for clarification.
Note taking should capture the structure and the key points, not every word that is spoken.
Precis writing and abstracting are the skills of compressing a passage without losing its meaning.
Writing a curriculum vitae
A curriculum vitae or resume is a written summary of a person's education, skills and experience.
It should be brief, clearly arranged and free of errors, because it is often read in a few seconds.
The usual order is personal details, education, skills, experience and references.
A cover letter goes with it and explains why the applicant is suitable for that particular position.
Rural sociology and social groups
Rural sociology studies the social life, institutions and problems of rural society.
A social group is a number of people in regular interaction who share a sense of belonging.
Primary groups such as the family are small and personal, while secondary groups are larger and more formal.
Social stratification places people in layers by caste, class and occupation, and it shapes rural life closely.
Culture and social institutions
Culture is the learned way of life of a society, including its beliefs, values, customs and material objects.
Folkways are the customary ways of behaving, and mores are the stronger norms whose violation is seriously disapproved.
A taboo is a prohibition that is strongly held, and a ritual is a prescribed form of behaviour for an occasion.
Family, marriage, religion and education are the main social institutions through which culture is transmitted.
Social control and social change
Social control is the means by which a society brings its members to conform to its norms.
The means range from informal ones such as praise, ridicule and gossip to formal ones such as law and the police.
Social change is the alteration in the social structure and relationships over time.
In rural India the main forces of change are education, migration, technology and government programmes.
Educational psychology and perception
Educational psychology studies how people learn, and applies that understanding to teaching.
Sensation is the raw response of a sense organ, while perception is the meaning the mind gives to it.
Attention is the selective focusing of the mind, and it is the gateway through which learning enters.
Attitude is a learned tendency to respond in a favourable or unfavourable way to an object or idea.
Milestones in microbiology
Microbiology is the study of organisms too small to be seen with the unaided eye.
The theory of abiogenesis held that life arose spontaneously from non-living matter.
Louis Pasteur's experiments disproved abiogenesis and established the germ theory of disease.
Robert Koch gave the postulates that link a specific microorganism to a specific disease.
The light microscope
Magnification is the number of times an object is enlarged by the lenses of the microscope.
Resolving power is the ability to show two closely placed points as separate, and it sets the useful limit of magnification.
Numerical aperture measures the light-gathering ability of the objective lens and determines the resolving power.
Good illumination and correct focusing matter more for seeing detail than magnification alone.
The microbial world
Whittaker's five kingdom system divides living organisms into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Prokaryotes lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, and include bacteria and cyanobacteria.
Eukaryotes have a true nucleus and organelles, and include fungi, protozoa and algae.
Viruses are placed outside these kingdoms because they are not cellular and reproduce only inside a host.
Bacterial growth
Bacteria reproduce mainly by binary fission, in which one cell divides into two.
A growth curve has four phases: lag, log or exponential, stationary and death.
In the log phase the cells divide at the maximum rate for the conditions provided.
Temperature, pH, oxygen and nutrient supply decide the growth rate and the final population.
Livelihood and Indian agriculture
A livelihood is the way a person or household earns a living from the resources available to them.
Agriculture remains the largest source of livelihood in India and supports a very large share of the rural population.
Farm incomes are low and uneven because holdings are small and output depends on the monsoon.
A livelihood approach looks at the assets, activities and risks of the household as a whole.
Farming based livelihood systems
A farming system is the combination of enterprises and practices on a farm that together give the household its income.
A farming based livelihood system looks at the farm as one part of the household's wider set of activities.
The aim is to spread risk, use family labour fully and keep income flowing through the year.
The right combination depends on the agro-climatic zone, the size of the holding and the market available.
Components of a farming system
The main components are crops and cropping systems, livestock, poultry, fisheries and agroforestry.
Livestock such as dairy cattle, goats and poultry convert crop residues and common land into cash income.
By-products move between components: dung becomes manure for the crop and crop residues become feed.
This recycling lowers the cost of production and adds to the stability of the farm.
Risk, success factors and schemes
Farming based livelihoods face production risk from weather and pests and price risk from the market.
Diversification, insurance, credit and off-farm employment are the usual ways of managing that risk.
The success of an integrated system depends on the farmer's skill, the availability of inputs and the market link.
Central and state schemes provide support for irrigation, insurance, credit and market access.
Scope and branches of horticulture
Horticulture is the science and art of cultivating fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices and plantation crops.
Its main branches are pomology for fruits, olericulture for vegetables and floriculture for flowers.
Horticulture gives higher returns per unit area and uses labour intensively, which suits small holdings.
It also supplies raw material to the processing and export industries.
Plant propagation
Propagation is the multiplication of plants, and it is either sexual through seed or asexual through vegetative parts.
Sexual propagation gives variability and is used in breeding and for raising rootstocks.
Asexual propagation, such as cutting, layering, grafting and budding, keeps the characters of the parent exactly.
Seed dormancy is the state in which a viable seed does not germinate even when conditions appear suitable.
Orchard establishment and planting systems
Orchard establishment begins with the selection of the site, the crop and the planting material.
The layout decides where each tree is planted, and the common systems are square, rectangular, quincunx, triangular and hexagonal.
A system is chosen so that the available light and land are used efficiently.
Training shapes the young tree, and pruning removes unwanted growth to keep the canopy productive.
Fruitfulness and unfruitfulness
Bearing habit is the way a fruit tree carries its crop, such as on the current season's shoots or on spurs.
Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma, and it may be self or cross.
Unfruitfulness is the failure to set fruit, and it may be caused by poor pollination, an imbalance of nutrition or adverse weather.
Rejuvenation is the restoration of an old, unproductive orchard by pruning and renewed care.
Soil and its formation
Pedology studies soil as a natural body and its genesis, while edaphology studies soil as a medium for plant growth.
Soil is formed from rocks and minerals by weathering, which may be physical, chemical or biological.
The parent material, climate, relief, organisms and time are the five factors of soil formation.
Pedogenic processes such as addition, loss, translocation and transformation build the soil profile.
Soil profile and physical properties
A soil profile is a vertical section showing the horizons from the surface down to the parent material.
Soil texture is the proportion of sand, silt and clay, and it decides water holding and workability.
Soil structure is the arrangement of the particles into aggregates, which controls aeration and drainage.
Bulk density is the mass of dry soil per unit volume, and particle density is the density of the solid particles alone.
Soil colloids and ion exchange
Soil colloids are the very fine particles that give the soil its chemical activity.
They are inorganic, mainly the silicate clays, or organic, mainly the humus.
Because they carry negative charges, they hold positively charged ions on their surface.
Cation exchange capacity is the total amount of exchangeable cations the soil can hold, and base saturation is the share of those that are basic.
Silicate clays
Silicate clays are built from sheets of silica tetrahedra and alumina octahedra.
The 1 to 1 type, such as kaolinite, has little shrink-swell and a low exchange capacity.
The 2 to 1 type, such as montmorillonite, swells and shrinks strongly and holds more nutrients.
Isomorphous substitution, where one ion replaces another of similar size in the sheet, is the main source of charge in these clays.

t2_aen101.t: History of entomology and insect dominance
s: History of entomology and insect dominance
Insects are the most numerous group of animals, both in number of species and in number of individuals.
Their small size, ability to fly, short life cycle and high reproductive rate explain this dominance.
In India, entomology developed through the work of early economic entomologists and the establishment of research stations.
Insects matter to agriculture both as pests and as pollinators and natural enemies.
Insect morphology
The insect body is divided into the head, thorax and abdomen.
The head carries the antennae, the compound eyes and the mouthparts.
The thorax has three segments and bears the legs and, in most insects, two pairs of wings.
Mouthparts are modified for chewing, sucking, piercing, sponging or lapping, and this decides how a pest damages the crop.
Insect anatomy and physiology
The digestive system is a tube running from mouth to anus, with a crop and a gastric caeca.
Excretion is carried out mainly by the Malpighian tubules, which open into the hindgut.
Respiration takes place through spiracles and a network of tracheae that carry air directly to the tissues.
The nervous system is a chain of ganglia with a brain in the head, and the endocrine system controls moulting and metamorphosis.
Insect systematics
Insect taxonomy groups insects by their shared characters, using binomial nomenclature for naming.
A species is a group of individuals that interbreed freely and produce fertile offspring.
Genus, family and order are the higher categories used to place a species in the system.
The main orders of agricultural importance include Hemiptera, Lepidoptera, Coleoptera, Diptera, Hymenoptera and Orthoptera.
Personality and its determinants
Personality is the relatively stable pattern of behaviour, thought and feeling that makes a person distinct.
It is shaped by heredity, environment, culture and the person's own experiences.
Trait theories describe personality in terms of enduring characteristics that can be measured.
The humanistic approach emphasises the person's own drive towards growth and self-fulfilment.
Perception and attribution
Perception is the process by which a person selects, organises and interprets information from the world.
Individual behaviour is influenced more by what the person perceives than by the objective situation.
Attribution is the way we explain the causes of other people's behaviour.
A common error is to attribute our own failures to circumstance and other people's failures to their character.
Learning and its theories
Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour that comes from experience or practice.
Classical conditioning links a neutral stimulus with a response, as Pavlov showed in dogs.
Operant conditioning holds that behaviour is shaped by its consequences, especially reinforcement.
Social learning theory shows that people also learn by observing the behaviour of others and its results.
Motivation and group dynamics
Motivation is the force that starts, directs and sustains behaviour towards a goal.
Content theories, such as Maslow's hierarchy, ask what needs drive people.
Process theories, such as expectancy theory, ask how a person decides to put in effort.
In a group, a leader guides, norms govern behaviour and cohesion decides how well the members work together.
Agronomy and agroclimatic zones
Agronomy is the science and practice of crop production and soil management.
Its main concerns are the choice of crop and variety, the seedbed, nutrition, water and weed control.
An agroclimatic zone is an area with a broadly similar climate, soil and cropping pattern.
Zoning allows a recommendation to be matched to the tract where it will actually work.
Tillage and tilth
Tillage is the mechanical manipulation of the soil to prepare a seedbed and control weeds.
Tilth is the physical condition of the soil in relation to the growth of the crop.
Primary tillage opens the soil, and secondary tillage refines it for sowing.
Excessive tillage destroys structure and causes erosion, so the minimum needed is the right approach.
Crop nutrition
An essential nutrient is one that the plant cannot complete its life cycle without.
The criteria of essentiality require that the element is necessary for growth, cannot be replaced and acts within the plant.
Macronutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are needed in larger amounts than micronutrients.
Nutrients are absorbed as ions from the soil solution and by contact with the root surface.
Water and weed management
Soil moisture constants describe how strongly water is held in the soil.
Field capacity is the water retained after free drainage, and the permanent wilting point is the level at which the plant can no longer extract water.
The available water is the difference between those two, and irrigation is scheduled within that range.
A weed is a plant growing where it is not wanted, and it competes with the crop for water, nutrients, light and space.

t2_amp101.t: Livestock and poultry in the economy
s: Livestock and poultry in the economy
Livestock and poultry contribute milk, meat, eggs, wool, hides and draught power.
They provide regular income and employment, and act as insurance against crop failure.
The sector grows faster than crop agriculture and adds to the value of crop residues and common land.
The livestock census is the official count of animals, and it guides policy and planning.
Cattle breeds
Cattle breeds are classified as indigenous or exotic, and by their purpose as milch, draught or dual.
Indigenous milch breeds include Sahiwal, Red Sindhi and Gir, which are well adapted to local conditions.
Exotic milch breeds such as Holstein Friesian and Jersey give higher yields but need better management.
Crossbred animals combine the yield of the exotic parent with the hardiness of the indigenous one.
Digestion in ruminants
Ruminants such as cattle, buffalo, sheep and goats have a four-chambered stomach.
The rumen holds a dense population of microorganisms that break down cellulose the animal cannot digest itself.
Microbial action also synthesises B vitamins and helps in the use of non-protein nitrogen.
Poultry are non-ruminants and depend on a concentrated diet of grain, protein and minerals.
Poultry production
Poultry breeds are classified as layers for egg production and broilers for meat.
Commercial strains are selected for high egg number or for fast growth and good feed conversion.
Brooding, correct stocking density and clean water are essential in the early stage.
Vaccination against Ranikhet disease and other common infections is a routine part of poultry management.
Environment and its segments
The environment is the sum of all the living and non-living things that surround and affect an organism.
Its main segments are the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere.
Environmental studies is multidisciplinary, drawing on biology, chemistry, economics and social science.
Its central concern is the balance between human needs and the capacity of the environment.
Ecosystems
An ecosystem is a self-regulating unit in which living organisms interact with each other and with their surroundings.
Its structure has producers, consumers and decomposers, and its function is the flow of energy and the cycling of nutrients.
Energy flows in one direction, from the sun through producers to consumers, and is lost as heat at each level.
Biodiversity is the variety of life at the level of genes, species and ecosystems.
Environmental pollution
Pollution is the addition of a substance or energy to the environment in a harmful amount.
Air pollution comes mainly from industry, vehicles and the burning of crop residue and fuel.
Water pollution comes from sewage, industrial effluent and agricultural runoff carrying fertilizer and pesticide.
Control measures include treatment of waste, cleaner technology, and the three Rs of reduce, reuse and recycle.
Disaster management
A disaster is an event that causes widespread damage, loss of life and disruption beyond what the community can handle alone.
Natural disasters include floods, drought, cyclone, earthquake, landslide and forest fire.
The disaster management cycle runs through prevention and mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery.
For farmers, preparedness means storing seed and fodder, planning alternative crops and keeping insurance in place.
Plant pathogens
Plant pathology is the study of the diseases of plants, their causes and their management.
A disease is a deviation from normal functioning that causes damage and is expressed as symptoms.
The main pathogens are fungi, bacteria, viruses, viroids, phytoplasmas, nematodes and parasitic flowering plants.
The disease triangle explains that disease needs a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen and a favourable environment.
Fungi and their classification
Fungi are eukaryotic organisms that lack chlorophyll and obtain food from other organisms.
Their body is made of hyphae, and a mass of hyphae is called mycelium.
They reproduce by spores, which may be sexual or asexual, and which spread by wind, water and seed.
Modern classification places the fungal groups under the kingdoms Protozoa, Chromista and Fungi.
Bacteria, viruses and phytoplasmas
Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes, and plant pathogenic species often cause spots, blights and wilts.
Viruses are nucleoprotein particles that multiply only inside a living host cell and are spread by vectors or sap.
Phytoplasmas are wall-less bacteria that live in the phloem and are transmitted by leafhoppers.
A viroid is an even simpler agent, a small naked RNA, causing diseases such as potato spindle tuber.
Epidemiology and disease management
Epidemiology is the study of the development of disease in a population over time and space.
Weather, especially temperature, humidity and rainfall, strongly influences the build-up of an epidemic.
A pathogen survives between seasons in seed, soil, plant debris or an alternative host, and then spreads to the crop.
Management combines resistant varieties, clean seed, cultural practices, biological control and need-based fungicide.
Nutrient essentiality and deficiency
A nutrient is essential if the plant cannot complete its life cycle without it and no other element can replace it.
The role of a nutrient is specific, and its absence produces a characteristic deficiency symptom.
Nitrogen deficiency shows as general yellowing, beginning in the older leaves.
Toxicity occurs when a nutrient is present in excess, and it can be as damaging as a deficiency.
Soil testing and critical levels
Soil testing measures the available nutrient status and the reaction of the soil before the crop is sown.
A representative sample is the foundation of a reliable soil test, so sampling must be done correctly.
The critical level is the soil test value below which a response to the applied nutrient is expected.
The test result is interpreted with the crop and the yield target to build the recommendation.
Fertilizer recommendation approaches
A general recommendation gives a fixed dose for a crop, irrespective of the soil.
A soil test based recommendation adjusts the dose to the measured fertility of the field.
The soil test crop response approach uses field experiments to work out the dose for a target yield.
These approaches raise the efficiency of fertilizer use and reduce the cost and the loss to the environment.
Nutrient use efficiency
Nutrient use efficiency is the proportion of the applied nutrient that the crop actually takes up and uses.
It is low for nitrogen because of leaching, volatilisation and denitrification losses.
Splitting the dose, placing it in the root zone, and using the right source at the right time all raise efficiency.
Integrated nutrient management combines organic sources with the balance of chemical fertilizer that the soil needs.
Farm Management: Meaning and Concept
What is Farm Management? Farm management is that branch of agricultural economics which deals with the organisation and operation of a farm as a business unit.
It is important at the very outset to see that farm management is not merely a collection of improved practices.
How to produce - the choice of technology and of the proportions in which resources are combined.
The distinguishing feature of the farm firm is that its production is biological.
The farm manager therefore works with a technology that is partly within and partly beyond human control, which is why farm management has often been called an art as much as a science.

Inputs/resources: Factors used in the production process are known as inputs or resources.

The type of farming refers to the kind of enterprises a farm carries and the relative importance of each in the farm's income.

The most important examinable topic of this lecture is the family of seven cost concepts developed by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) and used throughout Indian agricultural economics to esti
Each successive concept is a superset of the previous one - it adds one more item.
Learning exactly what each concept adds is the key to answering any question on this topic.
Cost A1 Cost A1 is the value of all actual paid-out (cash) costs incurred in production, whether on owned or leased land, excluding rent paid for leased-in land and excluding all imputed costs.
It is useful for judging short-run survival but ignores the value of the farmer's own resources.
Minimum loss principle
There can be two decision situations: 1) when selling price covers the average total cost and 2) when selling price is less than average total cost but more than average variable cost.
In short run, only variable costs are important in decision-making.
So the minimum of average variable cost is the shutdown point (Py=AVC).
This minimum price at which shutting down becomes the preferred alternative is the shutdown price.
While production should be maintained in the short run if selling price is above variable cost, it cannot be continued indefinitely unless selling price exceeds average total costs.
Importance of Cost
Understanding cost is central to farm management for the following reasons: 66.Profit measurement.
The CACP uses Cost C2 (and increasingly C2+50%) as the basis for recommending minimum support prices, so cost concepts directly affect the income of millions of farmers.
A farmer compares the cost and return of competing crops to decide what to grow.
Cost per unit of output (cost of production per quintal) is the basic measure of technical and economic efficiency.
Comparison of cost with price tells the farmer whether it is worth producing at all (the shut-down decision).
Break-even Point
Break-even analysis: total revenue and total cost cross at the break-even output.
Concept and formula The break-even point (BEP) is the level of output (or the level of price) at which total revenue equals total cost, so that the farmer makes neither profit nor loss.
Because total cost has a fixed part and a variable part, we can write: At break-even: Total Revenue (TR) = Total Cost (TC) i.e.

If the farmer's expected yield is 80 quintals, he is above break-even and will earn a profit of (80 66.67) × 600 = ₹8,000.
Shut-down Point
Concept and rule The shut-down point is the level of price (or output) below which the farmer is better off stopping production in the short run rather than continuing.
It is a short-run decision, because in the short run the farmer is already committed to his fixed costs.

Net farm income is the true profit of the farm business and is the single most important measure of profitability.

Family Labour Income Family Labour Income = Net Farm Income + Imputed value of family labour This measure adds back the imputed value of family labour to net farm income, because family labour is not a cash cost.
It is the most complete measure of what the farm business earns for the family that runs it.
Economies of Scale and Size
The meaning of economies An economy is a cost advantage - a reduction in the average cost of production obtained as the farm grows or as the industry grows.
The opposite - an increase in average cost as size increases - is called a diseconomy.

It is important at the outset to separate two terms that are often used interchangeably but are not identical: Economies of scale refer to cost advantages obtained when all inputs are increased in the same proportio

Economies of size is a broader Indian usage referring to cost advantages from increasing the size of the farm business by any means, including better technology, better management and fuller use of existing capacity
They are the result of the farmer's own decisions and are under his control.

Isoquant or Iso-product curve
Isoquant is also known as iso-product curve or equal product or product indifference curve.
An isoquant is convenient device for compressing the three dimensional picture of a production function into two dimensions.
Isoquant is a curve showing all possible combinations of two inputs that result in equal amount of output.
Each point on an isoquants is the maximum output that can be achieved with given input combinations (X & X ).
The curve representing all combinations X1 and X2 inputs that produce a given of output is called an isoquant.
Imperfect substitution
Imperfect substitution: The two inputs are imperfect substitutes, MRTS declines (negative) and the isoquant is convex.
Kinked isoquant: When there is limited substitutability between the two inputs, the isoquant is a kinked one.
That is, there is only limited number of processes for producing a commodity.
Each process is represented by a straight line and passes through the origin.
Substitution between the inputs is possible only at the kinks.
Iso-cost line (price line)
The line showing all possible combination of two inputs that can be purchased with given amount of money is known as iso-cost line.
Each point on the iso-cost line represents a combination of inputs that can be purchased with the same outlay of funds.
Iso cost is otherwise called as equal cost lines, price line or outlay line.

The slope of the iso-cost line indicates the ratio of factor prices Expansion path The line or curve connecting the points of least cost combination for different levels of output is called expansion path.
Expansion path is an isocline, on which the slope of iso-quant (MRTS) equals the slope of iso-cost line (price ratio).
When the expansion path is a straight line starting from the origin, it implies that the inputs will be used in the same proportion at all output levels and hence it is called scale line.
On the other hand, if the expansion path is curved, it implied that the inputs will be used in various proportions.
The problem here is to find out a combination of inputs, which should cost the least, i.e., minimization of cost.

When profit is impossible Sometimes a farmer cannot make a profit under any combination - for example, when prices are depressed or resources are fixed and must be used.
In such situations the correct objective is not to maximise profit but to minimise loss.

Opportunity Cost Principle
If an input is used in a particular production process, it has no alternative use at that particular point of time.
This means that the input will be loosing income from the alternative use and this income foregone by this input from its alternative use is called opportunity cost.
By definition, opportunity cost is the income that could have been received, if the input had been used in its most profitable alternative use.
Alternatively, it is the value of product not produced because the input was used for another purpose.
Real cost of an input is not the purchase price of the input.

Enterprise Combination, Diversification and Risk
A farmer who grows only one crop earns the highest expected return if prices are favourable but bears the full risk of a price crash, pest attack or drought.
By combining enterprises that are not perfectly competitive - for example a crop with a dairy unit, or two crops with different seasons - the farmer reduces the variability of total income.
This is the risk-reduction motive for diversification, distinct from the pure profit motive.

What is farm business analysis? Farm business analysis is the systematic study of the farm as a business unit, using the farmer's records and physical observations, to measure its income, its efficiency and its prof
Its purpose is diagnostic and prescriptive: it tells the farmer not only how well he is doing but where he is losing money and how to improve.
Gross farm income is the total value of production and other farm receipts.
Net farm income is gross income minus total cost (including imputed costs).
Farm business income is the return to the operator's own labour, capital and land.
Measure Formula Meaning
Technical efficiency Technical efficiency is concerned with the physical relationship between input and output - how much output is obtained per unit of input, regardless of prices.
A farm is technically efficient when it obtains the maximum possible output from a given set of inputs, or the minimum inputs for a given output.
Mortality rate - lower mortality means better technical management.

A farm is economically efficient when it uses resources so as to maximise profit - that is, when inputs are combined and outputs chosen according to the price conditions (MVP = MFC, MRPS = price ratio).
Conversely, a modest yield may be economically efficient if costs are low.

Book-keeping is the art of recording business transactions in a set of books.
Under this system only the personal accounts of debtors and creditors and the cash account are maintained.
Real accounts (assets) and nominal accounts (expenses, incomes) are largely ignored.

Only one aspect of each transaction is recorded - for example, when ₹5,000 of fertiliser is bought for cash, only the cash payment is noted, not the corresponding change in fertiliser stock or expense.

Farm Planning: Meaning and Importance

Farm planning is the process of deciding, in advance, what the farm will produce, how it will produce it, and with what combination of resources, so as to achieve the farmer's objectives - usually maximum profit, bu
It is the intellectual work of choosing among alternatives before the resources are committed.
Planning is needed because resources (land, labour, capital, water) are scarce and have alternative uses, and because every choice has consequences that stretch over months or years.

A farm plan is not a single decision but a package: the crop and livestock enterprises to be taken, their area or numbers, the rotations to be followed, the input levels, the labour and machinery schedule, and the f
A plan tells the farmer exactly how much credit is needed, when, and for what - improving loan applications and repayment.
Importance of farm planning
A plan tells the farmer exactly how much credit is needed, when, and for what - improving loan applications and repayment.
Crop rotation, green manuring and conservation practices are incorporated into the plan, preserving productivity.
A written plan is the basis on which extension workers and banks advise and finance the farmer.
Planning is broader - it covers resources, timing, financing, risk and family needs.
Another error is to think planning is a one-time exercise;
Steps in Farm Planning
Gather data on the farm's resources (land area and quality, water, labour, machinery, capital), past yields and prices, and the farmer's objectives and family needs.
Prepare a resource inventory (see Lecture 11) listing every resource with its quantity, quality, timing of availability and cost.
List the crop and livestock enterprises that the soil, climate and market permit, together with their input-output relationships.
Using budgeting and programming techniques, choose the enterprises and their levels that best meet the objectives within resource limits.
Decide area under each crop, number of animals, rotations, input doses, machinery and labour schedules, and the calendar of operations.

It is used when the change affects only part of the business - for example, replacing one crop with another on a few hectares, changing a fertiliser dose, buying a small implement, or changing the method of harvesti
It is quick, requires little data, and needs no information about costs that remain unchanged.
A partial budget is prepared in four columns, grouped into two pairs: Column 1 - Added returns.
Net change in profit = (Added returns + Reduced costs) (Added costs + Reduced returns)− If the net change is positive, the change is profitable and should be adopted.
Budgeting: Meaning and Importance
A budget is a written statement, in physical and financial terms, of the expected income and expenditure of a farm or enterprise for a future period.
Where planning is the broad strategy, budgeting is the arithmetic that tests whether the strategy will work.
It estimates profitability in advance, allowing the farmer to reject unprofitable options before committing resources.
It compares alternatives on a common basis - a change of crop, a new implement, or a new enterprise can be judged by its effect on income and cost.
It reveals credit needs and their timing, because it lays out the cash flows month by month or season by season.

Complete (Whole-Farm) Budgeting
Complete budgeting, also called whole-farm budgeting, prepares an estimate of income and expenditure for the entire farm under an assumed plan.

It is used when the change 184 is large - a new cropping pattern, a shift from crop farming to dairying, or the addition of a major enterprise - so that partial budgeting cannot capture the interactions.
It is more laborious than partial budgeting because it re-plans every enterprise, but it is more accurate for major decisions and shows the whole farm's profitability, cash flow and resource use.

It is used when there are many competing enterprises and several scarce resources, so that budgeting by trial and error becomes difficult.

Meaning of Appraisal
Appraisal means the systematic assessment or evaluation of the farm's resources to determine their quantity, quality, timing of availability and cost, so that a sound plan can be built upon them.

It is the fact-finding step that precedes planning and budgeting: before a farmer can decide what to grow, the farmer must know exactly what land, labour, capital, machinery, buildings and water are available, how g
Appraisal answers four questions for every resource: How much? The quantity available (hectares, persons, rupees, litres per second).
These four dimensions - quantity, quality, timing and cost - form the framework for appraising every resource, and each is examined below.
A resource that is plentiful but costly, or cheap but available only at the wrong time, will not fit every enterprise.
Appraisal of Land
Its appraisal covers quantity, quality, timing (cropping season) and cost.
Parcel A is the best land (deep loam, assured irrigation) and should carry the most demanding, high-value crops.
Parcel C is rainfed with poor drainage and should carry hardy, low-risk crops or be put to fodder.
The average land value is ₹14,50,000 ÷ 4.5 = ₹3,22,222 per hectare.
Appraising only total area and ignoring quality and irrigation status - a hectare of rainfed clay is not the same as a hectare of irrigated loam.
Appraisal of Labour
Number of workers (family and permanent hired), expressed in man-days or man-equivalents (one adult male = 1 man-equivalent;
Total labour available = workers × working days per year.
Skilled labour (tractor driving, spraying, animal handling) is scarcer and costlier than unskilled labour.

Family labour is available all year, but peak operations (transplanting, harvesting) demand far more labour than the family can 204 supply, creating a peak-season deficit that must be met by hired labour.
The farm is self-sufficient in labour on an annual basis but faces a sharp peak-season deficit.
Appraisal of Capital
It is appraised as the sum of owned funds (net worth) and borrowed funds (credit), judged by quantity, quality (cost and terms), timing and cost.
Cheap, long-term institutional credit is superior to costly, short-term informal credit.
The farm can deploy ₹22,15,000 of capital, of which ₹3,00,000 is borrowed at an average cost of 8.3%.
Treating a sanctioned loan as available capital before it is actually disbursed.
Overlooking the repayment schedule, which affects cash flow even when the interest rate is low.
Appraisal of Machinery and Buildings
Machinery and implements (tractors, power tillers, ploughs, seed drills, threshers, sprayers, pumps) are appraised by: Quantity and capacity.
Number, power rating (hp/kW), width of work (m) and output (ha/hour).
Buildings (godowns, cattle sheds, poultry houses, implement sheds) are appraised by their capacity (tonnes or animals housed), condition, location and cost (depreciation, repairs, insurance).
If the farm's own area is small, custom hiring is usually cheaper than ownership.
Assuming full utilisation when the farm's area is small.
Appraisal of Water
Water is the most limiting resource in much of Indian agriculture.
Volume available per season, measured as discharge (litres per second) × hours of operation, or as canal water supply in acre-feet (1 acre-foot = 1,233 m³).
A tube-well yielding 30 l/s run 8 hours/day for 100 days delivers 30 × 8 × 3600 × 100 = 86.4 million litres = 86,400 m³ = about 70 acre-feet.
Availability relative to crop water requirement and the canal rotation (warabandi);
Assuming water is available whenever needed, ignoring the canal rotation.
Physical versus Financial Appraisal
Physical appraisal measures resources in physical units - hectares, man-days, horsepower, litres per second, tonnes of storage - and answers what the farm can technically do.
Financial appraisal measures resources in money - value of land, wage bill, machinery cost, cost of irrigation - and answers what the farm can afford and what it earns.
Appraisal must therefore present the physical resource base first, then value it.
Criteria for Selection of Crops
The selection should be guided by a set of criteria, each of which is a likely exam point.
A balance between subsistence and commercial crops is desirable.
On gross margin per hectare, onion is the most profitable.
But when water is the limiting resource, gross margin per water unit is the correct criterion, and onion (₹13,750) and maize (₹12,250) rank above paddy (₹7,188).
The choice therefore depends on which resource is limiting - a key insight.

s: Criteria for Selection of Livestock Enterprises
Livestock (dairy, buffalo, poultry, goat, sheep, piggery) add income, use family labour and farm by-products, and provide regular cash flow.
Compare on net return per animal and per rupee invested, or on the benefit-cost ratio.
For dairy, use net return per milch animal per lactation;
Dairy and poultry are labour-intensive and need daily attention;
goat and sheep are less demanding and suit labour-scarce farms.
Matching Resources to Enterprises
The final step is to match the appraised resources to the selected enterprises so that the whole farm plan is internally consistent.
Matching is done resource by resource: Land - allocate the best land to the most demanding, high-value crops;
avoid enterprises needing machinery the farm lacks (unless custom hiring is feasible).
A well-matched plan uses every resource at its best and leaves no resource idle in one season while another is short.
It is the practical synthesis of appraisal (this lecture) and planning (Lecture 10): the resource inventory feeds the plan, and the plan is judged by how well it matches the resources.
Risk and Uncertainty
In everyday language the two words are used interchangeably, but in economics and farm management they carry a precise and different meaning.
Knight in his 1921 book Risk, Uncertainty and Profit, and it is Knight's distinction that all subsequent literature follows.

Risk refers to a situation in which the outcome of a decision is unknown, but the probability distribution of possible outcomes is known, or can be estimated with reasonable accuracy from past experience.
The outcomes are uncertain, but their probabilities are knowable.
Uncertainty (sometimes called true or Knightian uncertainty) refers to a situation in which the outcome is unknown and the probability distribution itself is unknown or cannot be estimated.
Measurability and Insurability
The practical consequence of measurability is insurability, and this is the single most important link between this lecture and the next.
Insurance works by pooling many independent exposure units so that the losses of the few are met from the premiums of the many.
For this to be actuarially possible, the insurer must be able to estimate the probability and the likely magnitude of loss.
A useful intermediate category is partly measurable risk, where some but not all of the probability distribution is known.
Government intervention (as in PMFBY, discussed in Lecture 13) is often justified precisely to cover those parts of the risk that the private market will not underwrite.
Basis of distinction Risk Uncertainty
Do not say that risk is "small uncertainty" or that uncertainty is "large risk".
The distinction is qualitative - it is about whether a probability can be attached to outcomes - not about the size of the possible loss.
A very large potential loss with known probability is still risk;
a modest potential loss with no estimable probability is uncertainty.
Nature of Risk in Agriculture
Agriculture is widely regarded as one of the riskiest of all economic activities, and the reasons are intrinsic to farming rather than incidental to it.
Yield is determined jointly by the farmer's inputs and by weather, pest and disease events that the farmer cannot control.
A crop decision taken at sowing is vindicated or destroyed only months later at harvest.
Output arrives in a lump at harvest, when prices are typically lowest (the "harvest price dip"), and produce is often perishable, forcing distress sales.
Because demand for food is inelastic, small supply changes produce large price swings.
Production or Natural Risk
This arises from variability in yield caused by factors beyond the farmer's control.
It includes: Weather variability - drought, floods, excess or deficit rainfall, hailstorm, frost, heat waves, unseasonal rain.
Example: unseasonal rain and hailstorms in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh in early 2015 destroyed standing rabi wheat and gram, causing widespread crop loss.
Production risk is the classic measurable risk and is the primary target of crop and livestock insurance.
Price or Market Risk This is variability in the price at which output is sold (and inputs bought).
Technological Risk
Risk arising from the adoption of new technology whose performance is not yet proven on the farmer's own field.

Example: a farmer who shifts to a new high-yielding variety or a new machine may find that the variety performs poorly under local conditions, or that the machine's repair and spare-part support is inadequate.
Technological risk is closer to uncertainty because reliable local probability data usually do not exist at the time of adoption.
It is also the risk of obsolescence - a costly asset may become outdated.
Personal or Human Risk
Risk arising from the human element in the farm business: Illness, accident or death of the farmer or a family member, disrupting operations and earning capacity.
Labour problems - shortage at peak season, strikes, or unreliability of hired labour.
Management failure - poor decisions, lack of skills, or fraud by an employee or partner.
Example: the sudden death of the principal decision-maker in a smallholding often forces distress sale of assets because no succession or contingency plan exists.
Institutional or Policy Risk
Financial Risk Risk arising from the way the farm is financed: Borrowing risk - the obligation to repay debt (principal plus interest) regardless of the season's outcome.
Credit availability risk - the danger that a needed loan is refused or delayed, or that a renewal of the crop loan (KCC) is not sanctioned.
Financial risk is often the channel through which other risks become catastrophic: a yield or price shock that would merely reduce income for a debt-free farmer can bankrupt a heavily indebted one.
This is central to understanding farmer distress in India.

Keep the categories straight: ask what is varying - yield (production), price (market), the performance of a new technology (technological), the human factor (personal), the policy environment (institutional), or th
Expected Value (Mean)
The expected value is the probability-weighted average of the possible outcomes.
E(X) = Σ (Pi × Xi) where E(X) = expected value of the variable X;
The expected value summarises the central tendency - the average outcome the farmer can expect over many repetitions.
Variance Variance measures the average squared deviation of outcomes from their expected value.
(Xi E(X)) = deviation of outcome i from the mean.− Because deviations are squared, both positive and negative deviations contribute positively to variance, and large deviations are weighted heavily.
Standard Deviation
The standard deviation is simply the positive square root of the variance, and it is expressed in the same units as the original variable (rupees, quintals), which makes it directly interpretable.
Standard deviation (σ) = [ Σ Pi (Xi E(X))² ]√ − where σ = standard deviation;
Between two plans with the same expected return, the one with the lower σ is preferred by a risk-averse farmer.
Coefficient of Variation
The standard deviation is an absolute measure and cannot be used to compare variability between distributions with different means or different units.
The coefficient of variation 223 (CV) standardises dispersion as a percentage of the mean, so it is a relative measure of risk.
Coefficient of variation (CV) = (σ / E(X)) × 100 where CV = coefficient of variation expressed as a percentage;
The plan with the lower CV has less risk per unit of expected return, and is generally preferred.
CV is the most useful single measure when comparing enterprises of different scale or value, such as wheat versus dairy.
