Note that although Plan B has a slightly lower absolute standard deviation, its relative variability (CV) is higher, and its mean is lower.
Mixing units: variance is in ₹², standard deviation in ₹, and CV is a percentage.
Comparing CVs computed with different means as if they were absolute risk.
CV is a ratio and must be interpreted as risk per rupee of return.
Risk Management Strategies
Farmers and policymakers use a range of tools to reduce, transfer or absorb risk.
These are conveniently grouped into production, marketing, financial and general/institutional strategies.

Production Strategies These aim to reduce or spread production risk at source: Diversification - growing several crops, or combining crop with livestock, poultry, fishery or agro-forestry, so that a failure in one e
Diversification works best when enterprises' returns are not perfectly positively correlated.
Storage and warehousing - using warehouses (including negotiable warehouse receipts under the WDRA) to sell in the off-season when prices are higher.
Financial Strategies
These aim to reduce the risk of the financing structure itself: Maintaining financial reserves and liquidity - holding cash or easily liquidated assets to meet shocks.
Insurance - crop, livestock and machinery insurance to transfer risk to an insurer (the subject of Lecture 13).
Debt management and avoiding over-capitalisation - keeping leverage within prudent limits, matching loan tenure to the income stream, and using crop loans rather than informal high-cost debt.
Credit reserves - arranging an unused line of credit for emergencies.
Enterprise accounting and budgeting - knowing costs and returns so that borrowing is planned, not reactive.
General / Institutional Strategies
These operate through the wider institutional environment: Government support programmes - MSP and procurement, price stabilisation funds, market intervention schemes, and disaster relief.
Crop and livestock insurance schemes - PMFBY, WBCIS and livestock insurance (Lecture 13).
Institutional credit - Kisan Credit Card, interest subvention and timely credit to reduce dependence on moneylenders.
Extension, training and information - better information reduces uncertainty and improves decisions.
Farmer Producer Organisations and cooperatives - collective action to share risk and cost.
Strategy group Objective Representative tools
Exam focus Key points to remember Risk is measurable and insurable;
Agriculture is inherently risky because of biological production, long time-lags, seasonality, inelastic demand, small scale and incomplete markets.
Expected value, variance, standard deviation and coefficient of variation are the standard measures of variability;
CV is the relative measure used to compare plans of different scale.

Its objectives are: To provide comprehensive risk cover to farmers from pre-sowing to post-harvest, against non-preventable natural risks.
For the North-Eastern states and Himalayan states, the sharing is 90 per cent Centre : 10 per cent State.

Livestock Insurance
Livestock is a major source of income and a store of wealth for Indian farmers, especially the landless and smallholders.
It is a form of asset insurance rather than yield insurance.
Key features: 241 Cover is normally for the market value of the animal (or a fixed sum insured based on breed, age and productivity), and the policy term is typically one year, renewable.
Identification of the insured animal is essential - usually by ear-tag, brand or, increasingly, by RFID tags and photographs - to prevent fraudulent claims on uninsured animals.

Livestock insurance is especially important because a single animal's death can represent a large loss relative to a smallholder's income, and because the productive asset is also the household's savings.
Machinery Insurance
It is closely analogous to motor or engineering insurance.
Sum insured is based on the machine's value, often on a depreciated (market) value or, for new machines, on the invoice value.
Premium is generally a small percentage of the insured value, and may be reduced by no-claim bonuses.
Machinery insurance is important because farm machines are costly, are used in rugged conditions, and are often financed by loans;

The Pilot Crop Insurance Scheme
Dandekar‗s suggestion, GIC prepared a crop insurance scheme based on the area approach and put it into operation from 1979-80.
Initially, it was introduced as a pilot scheme in three States and was extended to twelve States by 1984-85.
The insurance premium ranged from 5-10 per cent of the sum insured.
The number of farmers covered in a year ranged from 16,000 to 60,000, except for 1984-85, when 4, 47,000 were covered.
The loss ratio was 1.10 over the five-year period from 1979-80 to 1980-84.
The Comprehensive Crop Insurance Scheme (CCIS)
The Government of India introduced CCIS in the financial year 1985-86.
Operated by GIC in collaboration with the respective State governments, the scheme covered cereals, pulses and oilseeds.
farmers who availed themselves of loans for specified crops were eligible for insurance coverage.
State governments were left to decide whether to operate the scheme in the State or not.
This is in contrast of the rate of 5-10 per cent in the pilot crop insurance scheme.
The National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS)
Like CCIS, NAIS is primarily based on the area approach.
It envisages coverage of cereals, millets, pulses, oilseeds and annual horticultural/commercial crops for which adequate yield data are available.
Premium rates: The premium rates are 3.5 per cent for oilseeds and bajra and 2.5 per cent for cereals, millets and pulses during Kharif;
The rates for annual commercial/horticultural crops are based on actuals.
Premium subsidy: Premiums for small/marginal farmers are subsidized to the extent of 50 per cent, to be shared equally between the Centre and States.
Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (WBCIS)
The basic approach of ―weather index‖ insurance is to estimate the percentage deviation in crop output due to adverse deviations in weather conditions.
There are crop models and statistical techniques available to work out the correlation between crop output and weather parameters.
For loss estimation, a Reference Unit Area (RUA) is deemed to be a homogenous area unit of insurance.
Each RUA is linked to a Reference Weather Station (RWS);
claims are determined on the basis of weather data recorded by the RWS.
National Crop Insurance Programme (NCIP)
In the new programme, WBCIS, MNAIS and Coconut Palm Insurance Scheme (CPIS) are included as full-fledged schemes with certain modifications over their pilots.
Farmers are entitled to maximum premium subsidy up to 50 per cent under WBCIS and 75 per cent under MNAIS on a graded scale.

Premium rates have been capped according to the type of crop and season, and in cases where the actuarial premium rates are higher than the capped limit, the sum insured for such crops will be reduced in proportion
The scheme is being implemented on a regular basis from 2008-09 in 100 newly selected districts of the country.
Under the scheme, the crossbred and high yielding cattle and buffaloes are being insured at maximum of their current market price.

d25_econ231.t: Scope and Importance of Resource Economics
s: Scope and Importance of Resource Economics
Resource economics is of great practical importance in India.

Agriculture depends heavily on natural resources - land, water, soil and biodiversity - many of which are degraded: groundwater tables are falling in the north-western states, soils are losing fertility, forests and
Because these resources are scarce, shared, and often unpriced, they tend to be overused.
It is thus indispensable for framing policies on irrigation, watershed development, forest management and sustainable agriculture - the subjects of the following lectures.

Natural Resource Economics and Agricultural Economics: A Comparison Natural resource economics and agricultural economics are closely related - both deal with land, water and biological production - but they differ
Definition of Natural Resources

A natural resource may be defined as any material, energy or environmental amenity occurring in nature that is useful to human beings and can be used to satisfy wants or to produce goods and services.
It is provided by nature (not created by human effort), though its usefulness may depend on technology and human knowledge.
It is useful - it satisfies a human want or assists production.
It is (usually) scarce - available in limited quantity relative to demand, so that its use involves a cost or a choice.
The last point is crucial: something is a resource only if it is both useful and scarce.
Renewable versus Non-renewable Resources
Renewable resources are those that can be replenished by natural processes within a humanly relevant time scale, provided the rate of use does not exceed the rate of regeneration.
Examples: solar energy, wind, forests (if harvested sustainably), fisheries, soil fertility, groundwater (if recharge exceeds extraction), and livestock and crops.
Renewable resources are further divided into: Flow (continuous) renewables - those whose supply is essentially continuous and unaffected by use, e.g.
Non-renewable resources are those whose stock is fixed and which are not replenished within a human time scale;
Their central economic problem is the optimal rate of depletion - how fast to use a finite stock.
Exhaustible versus Inexhaustible Resources
Exhaustible resources can be used up - their total stock is finite.
Both non-renewable resources (coal, minerals) and stock-flow renewables (groundwater in a depleted aquifer, a fishery being overfished) can be exhaustible if used beyond their regeneration capacity.
Inexhaustible resources are available in effectively unlimited quantity and cannot be used up by human activity, e.g.
solar energy, wind, tidal energy, and (in normal circumstances) air and sea water.
Note that even "inexhaustible" resources can be 253 degraded in quality - air and water can be polluted - which is why quality, not just quantity, matters.
Recyclable versus Non-recyclable Resources
Recyclable resources are those that can be recovered and reused after use, so that the effective stock is extended, e.g.
Non-recyclable resources cannot be recovered or reused once consumed - they are dissipated or transformed irreversibly.
Examples: coal, petroleum and natural gas (which are burnt and converted to gases), and nuclear fuel.
For these, conservation and substitution are the only long-run strategies.
A forest, fishery or aquifer is renewable only if the rate of harvest does not exceed the rate of regeneration.
Unique Properties of Natural Resources
The 254 economic problem is therefore one of allocation across time - how much to use now and how much to leave for the future.
Natural resources cannot be moved to where they are wanted;
A mineral deposit, a forest or an aquifer is fixed in place, so transport cost and local availability shape their use.
Land, in particular, is completely immobile - its value depends heavily on location.
Natural resources are not uniform: no two plots of land, no two aquifers and no two forests are identical in quality.

d25_econ231.t: Hotelling's Rule and a Worked Example
s: Hotelling's Rule and a Worked Example
Hotelling's rule states that the owner of an exhaustible resource is indifferent between extracting a unit now and extracting it later, provided the resource rent grows at the rate of interest.
Suppose the resource rent on a mineral deposit is ₹1,000 per tonne today and the interest rate is 8 per cent per year (r = 0.08).

Because the rent is expected to rise by 8 per cent a year - exactly the interest rate - the owner is indifferent between selling the resource today and holding it for the future: the present value of a tonne sold in
If the rent is expected to rise faster than the interest rate, the rational owner delays extraction (keeps the resource in the ground);
if it is expected to rise slower than the interest rate, the owner extracts sooner.

d25_econ231.t: Optimal Depletion of an Exhaustible Resource
s: Optimal Depletion of an Exhaustible Resource
The optimal rate of depletion is the time path of extraction that maximises the present value of the total net benefit from the resource.

It balances two opposing forces: extracting sooner yields earlier benefits (valued more highly because of discounting), while extracting later preserves the resource for a time when its rent is higher.

The efficient rule is to extract at each date up to the point where the marginal benefit of an extra unit equals its marginal user cost - that is, until the rent rises at the rate of interest (Hotelling's rule).

s: Attributes or dimensions of natural resources
A natural resource is multi attribute in nature with different dimensions.
(3) Time: Natural resources are having time dimension and it refers to relative abundance or scarcity of resources at different point of time.
(4) Space: There is variation in the endowment of natural resources across region and round the world, but the demand for such resources is more or less uniform.
It can also be viewed as a flow of useful natural resource commodities or services which are produced from these stocks.
The stocks or reserves indicate what is known to be available for future use, while the flow of commodities and services from the stocks indicate the level of current use.
Importance of natural resources
Natural resources are directly consumed as in the case of fresh fish, water, outdoor recreation, and firewood;
It may also be used as inputs in the intermediate processing such as iron or copper ores into smelting;
It also have consumptive uses in intermediate processing such as consumption of fuels in manufacturing and transport;
It is also having existence value or in situ uses like free-running rivers, parks, and wilderness areas with its rich flora and fauna.
In some cases, these modes of utilization can be combined into multi-purpose natural resource systems that utilize resources simultaneously to satisfy several needs.
The Four Property Rights Regimes
The four property-rights regimes - the difference is who is excluded.

Economists classify resource ownership into four broad regimes, distinguished by two questions: who owns the resource (an identifiable group or no one) and how access is controlled (regulated or unregulated).
These four regimes are private property, common property, state property and open access.
Private Property
Under private property, the resource is owned by an individual or a corporate entity, who can exclude others, use it as they wish (within the law), and transfer it.
The owner bears the full cost and receives the full benefit of use, so incentives are aligned with conservation.
Examples: an owned field, a privately owned well, a plantation, a private pond, a tractor.
Private property is generally associated with efficient use because the owner internalises both benefits and costs - but it can also lead to under-provision of 263 public benefits (e.g.
an owner may not maintain a forest for its watershed value) and to inequity where ownership is highly concentrated.
Common Property

Under common property, the resource is owned and used by a defined and limited group of people - a village community, a user group, a cooperative - who share rights to use it according to agreed rules, and who can e
The distinguishing feature is that access is limited to the members of the group and regulated by rules, norms or institutions.
Examples: village grazing land (gauchar), community forests, village ponds and tanks, shared irrigation channels, and traditional fishing grounds with customary rules.

Because members can exclude outsiders and regulate each other's use, common property can be managed sustainably - a point emphasised by Elinor Ostrom, who showed that communities often devise effective rules for sel
State Property
Under state property, the resource is owned and controlled by the government, which may regulate access and use, grant concessions, or prohibit use altogether.
Examples: reserved forests, national parks and sanctuaries, major rivers, mineral deposits, and government canals.
State ownership can protect resources that no individual would conserve (e.g.
biodiversity), but it can also fail when the state lacks the capacity to enforce rules, and it may exclude local communities who depend on the resource, sometimes producing conflict and illegal use.
Open Access
Under open access (or no property, res nullius), there is no effective ownership or control - no one can be excluded, and no rules govern use.
Open access is the classic cause of overexploitation and degradation, because no user has an incentive to conserve: whatever one user leaves will simply be taken by another.
This is the setting for the "tragedy of the commons" (more precisely, the tragedy of open access).
The word "common" is often used loosely to mean "open to all".
In economics, common property is the opposite of open access: common property has a defined group of owners and rules of use, whereas open access has no owners and no rules.
Common Property Resources: Meaning

Common Property Resources (CPRs) are resources that are owned and used by a well- defined community or group of users, who share rights of use according to a set of rules or norms, and who can exclude non-members.
A CPR is thus a resource under a common property regime - neither privately owned by an individual nor open to all.
Rules of use - customs, norms or formal rules governing how much each member may use, when, and how the resource is maintained and protected.

This "partial excludability" is what distinguishes a CPR from private property (fully excludable) and from open access (fully non-excludable).

d25_econ231.t: Common Property versus Open Access: The Crucial Distinction
s: Common Property versus Open Access: The Crucial Distinction
The distinction between common property and open access is one of the most important in resource economics and is frequently misstated.
Both involve resources used by many people, but they differ fundamentally in whether access is limited and regulated.
The "tragedy of the commons" described by Garrett Hardin in 1968 is often cited to argue that shared resources must be privatised or nationalised.
Thus the policy question is not "private or shared?" but "how can effective rules and boundaries be established and maintained?" Common mistake.
Similarly, do not say CPRs are "owned by the government" - that is state property.

d25_econ231.t: Property Rights, Incentives and Investment: An Illustration
s: Property Rights, Incentives and Investment: An Illustration
The link between property rights and economic behaviour is best seen through a simple investment decision.
The investment is worthwhile only if the farmer can expect to reap the returns over that period.
The present value of the returns exceeds the cost, so the investment is made, and the resource base (water, soil) is improved.
With insecure or short-duration rights (a tenant on an annual, informal lease who may be evicted, or a farmer whose title is disputed), the farmer cannot be sure of reaping the returns.
The resource is degraded, and output is lower for everyone.
Common Property Resources
Common Property Resources (CPR) are those properties owned in common by identifiable group of people.
They are widely prevalent in India especially in semi-arid and arid regions, hill regions, forest and tribal regions.
In semi-arid and arid regions, the area under CPRs is very low but closely integrated with well-defined institutional setup.
In hill regions, the use of 273 CPR is high but ownership rights are defined not clearly while in forest tribal regions, the use of CPR is variable.
A Common Property Resources (CPRs) is a resource owned by a large group of individuals whose access to the resource can be limited or unlimited.
Characteristics of CPRs
CPRs have some significant characteristics, which distinguish from Private Property Resources (PPRs) or State Property Resources (SPRs) or Open Access Resources (OPRs).

Firstly, improperly defined individual private property rights, which lead, to the usage of the resource characterize it by more number of individuals as against the capacity of the resource system to sustain.
Secondly, the CPRs are characterized by joint use among the members of the community.
Whenever, resources are used jointly, members try to maximize their marginal private benefits and minimize their marginal private cost as against socially optimum benefits or costs.
Positive and Negative Externalities
A negative externality: the market produces too much and society suffers a welfare loss.
Positive Externalities
A positive externality arises when an activity benefits third parties who do not pay for the benefit.
Because the producer cannot capture the full benefit, too little of the activity is undertaken relative to the social optimum.

A farmer who plants trees provides shelter, reduces wind erosion, improves local rainfall and microclimate, and may recharge groundwater - benefits that spill over to neighbours and the community without payment.

Farmers who adopt contour bunding or check dams in an upper catchment reduce runoff and soil erosion, benefiting downstream farmers through better water availability and less siltation - a benefit they cannot charge
Because these benefits are not paid for, the private market under-provides them - a positive externality leads to under-production of the beneficial activity, which is also a form of inefficiency.
Negative Externalities
A negative externality arises when an activity imposes a cost on third parties who are not compensated.
Because the producer does not bear the full cost, too much of the activity is undertaken relative to the social optimum.
Because these costs are not paid by the producer, the activity is over-produced - a negative externality leads to over-production of the harmful activity, and hence to inefficiency.
If one farmer's larger output lowers the market price for all farmers, that is a price effect transmitted through the market, not a true externality.
A true externality is a direct, non-market effect on third parties' production or welfare (pollution, waterlogging), not one operating through prices.
Externalities, Open Access and Inefficiency

Both negative externalities and open access cause the same fundamental problem: the private decision-maker does not bear the full social cost of their actions, so they use the resource "too much", and society suffer
The mechanism is best seen with the standard cost diagram, explained in words below.

d25_econ231.t: The MPC / MSC Diagram Explained in Words
s: The MPC / MSC Diagram Explained in Words
But society's true cost is the higher MSC curve, which lies above the MPC curve by the amount of the external cost.
Society's optimum is where MSC equals marginal benefit - the socially optimal quantity, Qs, which is smaller than Qm.
The gap between Qm and Qs is the over-production caused by the externality.
Over that range, each extra unit produces a benefit to the firm that is less than the true social cost of producing it, so each such unit destroys value.
The total value destroyed - the area between the MSC curve and the marginal-benefit curve, over the range from Qs to Qm - 277 is the deadweight loss or welfare loss.
Welfare Loss
The welfare loss (deadweight loss) from an externality or from open access is the reduction in total social welfare that results because the level of activity differs from the social optimum.
Because the welfare loss is external to the decision-maker, it will not be corrected by the market on its own.
Correcting it requires internalising the externality - making the decision-maker face the full social cost or benefit of their actions - which is the task of the policy instruments discussed next.
Students sometimes say the market "fails" because firms are irrational or greedy.
The point is not greed but incentives: a firm that ignores an external cost is behaving rationally given the prices it faces.
Solutions to Externalities
There are four broad families of solutions, often used in combination.
Regulation (Command and Control) The government directly limits or prohibits harmful activities by law.
Examples: bans on stubble burning, restrictions on pesticide use, limits on groundwater extraction, standards for effluent discharge, and zoning laws.
Regulation is simple and direct, but it can be inflexible, costly to enforce, and uniform across situations that differ in cost.
Property Rights (Coasean Solutions)

The Coase theorem (after Ronald Coase) holds that if property rights are clearly defined, transaction costs are low, and parties can bargain, then the parties will negotiate an efficient outcome regardless of who in
In practice, however, transaction costs are often high (many affected parties, uncertain damages), so clear property rights help but do not always suffice.
Assigning rights - to land, water, forests - gives owners the incentive to conserve, because they capture the future benefit.
Examples: granting secure land titles, formalising community forest rights (the Forest Rights Act, 2006), and creating water rights.
Pricing and Market-Based Instruments

These make the externality part of the decision-maker's costs or revenues: Pigouvian tax - a tax equal to the marginal external cost, which raises the private cost to the social cost and reduces the activity to the
a tax on chemical fertilisers or on groundwater extraction).
Subsidy - a payment equal to the marginal external benefit, to encourage activities with positive externalities (e.g.
subsidies for tree planting, watershed works or organic farming).
Tradable permits (cap and trade) - a total limit is set and permits to pollute are traded, so that pollution reduction occurs where it is cheapest.
Collective Action
Where a resource is shared and externalities are mutual, collective action - cooperation among users - can internalise the externality directly.
Communities can devise and enforce rules limiting each member's use, share the costs of protection, and monitor compliance.
This is the approach emphasised by Elinor Ostrom, who showed that self- governance often works better than either pure state control or privatisation.
Collective action is discussed in detail in the management section below.
Also note that a tax is used for negative externalities and a subsidy for positive ones;
Management of Common Property Resources
Managing a CPR means establishing and enforcing rules so that use does not exceed sustainable levels, while preserving the access rights of the poor.
The management principles are similar across resource types - define boundaries, set rules, monitor, sanction, and resolve conflicts - but the specifics differ.
Management of Common Land

Common land (village commons, wastelands, threshing floors) is managed by community institutions - the Gram Panchayat, traditional village bodies, or user groups - that regulate grazing, fuelwood collection and encr
Measures include: Demarcation and protection of common land to prevent encroachment and illegal occupation.
Regulated grazing - rotational grazing, restrictions on the number of animals, and seasonal closures to allow regeneration.
WUAs are a cornerstone of Participatory Irrigation Management (PIM) in India.
Programmes such as the Integrated Watershed Management Programme and the Neeru-Meeru initiative in Andhra Pradesh are examples.
Management of Pastures
Common pastures are managed to prevent overgrazing, which degrades vegetation and soil: Carrying-capacity rules limiting the number of animals that may be grazed.
Rotational and deferred grazing - closing parts of the pasture in rotation so that grasses recover.
Fodder development - planting improved grasses and fodder trees, and encouraging stall-feeding to reduce grazing pressure.
Community enforcement - fines for violating grazing rules, imposed by the village body.
Management of Fisheries
Fisheries are managed to prevent overfishing and to protect breeding stocks: Community fishery rules - customary rules governing who may fish, where, when and with what gear.
Traditional fishing communities in Kerala and Tamil Nadu regulate fishing grounds, seasons and gear.
Seasonal closures - a closed season during the breeding period (e.g.
the annual fishing ban along India's coasts) to allow stocks to recover.
Mesh-size and gear restrictions - to avoid catching juvenile fish.
Management of Forests
JFM is a partnership institution - communities protect and manage forest land jointly with the Forest Department in exchange for a share of benefits - not merely a plantation programme.
Likewise, a WUA is an institution for allocating water and maintaining infrastructure, not just a group of farmers.

The opposite is true if the benefits are delayed, remote, hard to identify and do not accrue to the investors of efforts.
The less renewable a resource is the more risk there is that poor management will have drastic consequences, and the more reason one can offer for some form of government involvement.
Seasonality is another factor of great importance for resource management.
Examples from Botswana, Philippines, Indonesia, and Nepal suggest that the flow of local institutional activity is generally affected by variations in the agricultural season.
During wet season, water is abundant and it needs less co-operative efforts for water management and maintenance.
Land Resources
Common property land resource refers to lands identified with a specific type of property rights.

The common lands covered in the National Sample Survey (NSS) enquiry are panchayat lands, government revenue lands, village common lands, village thrashing lands, unclassified forest lands, woodlands and wastelands,
Forest & Pasture Resources

Common property resources, particularly forests and pastures are rapidly decreasing and deteriorating in developing countries like Nepal resulting in many unintended and unanticipated environmental problems.

Unclassified forests, with very low productivity, are always open to use by local communities: Accordingly, both protected and unclassified forests are treated as forming a part of common property forest resources.
It is, therefore, the subset of total forest area minus reserve forests to which common property rights are assumed to exist.
Water Resources 289 There are a variety of resources of water, which are in the public domain, and a significant part of these are included in the category of commons.
Examples are flows of rivers, tanks and natural lakes, groundwater, wetland and mangrove areas, and such other water bodies.
Extension education
Extension education is the process of bringing about desirable changes in the knowledge, skill and attitude of rural people.
It is informal, voluntary and based on the needs of the people themselves.
The extension worker acts as a guide and a catalyst rather than as a director.
The extension process moves from the collection of facts, through analysis and decision, to action and review.
Extension system in India
Early extension efforts included the Sriniketan and Marthandam projects and the Gurgaon experiment.
After independence, the community development programme and the national extension service were launched.
The training and visit system later reorganised the extension machinery around regular farmer contact.
Today extension is delivered through state departments, agricultural universities and the Krishi Vigyan Kendra.
Rural development programmes
Rural development aims to improve the economic and social life of the rural population.
Programmes have addressed employment, irrigation, housing, credit, health and rural infrastructure.
Monitoring checks progress against the plan, and evaluation judges the outcome against the objective.
Farmer producer organisations and self-help groups are the newer vehicles for rural development.
Diffusion of innovations
An innovation is an idea or practice that is new to the individual or the community.
Diffusion is the process by which an innovation spreads among the members of a social system over time.
Adopters are classified as innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards.
Adoption passes through the stages of awareness, interest, evaluation, trial and adoption.
Kharif cereals: rice
Rice is the most important kharif cereal of India and is grown mainly under transplanted lowland conditions.
It needs high temperature, high humidity and assured water, and is suited to heavy soils that hold water.
The crop is raised by raising a nursery and transplanting 20 to 25 day old seedlings, or by direct sowing.
Water management and timely nitrogen top dressing are the main levers on yield.
Kharif pulses
The main kharif pulses are pigeon pea, mung bean, urd bean and horse gram.
They are deep-rooted legumes that fix nitrogen and improve the soil for the following crop.
Pigeon pea is a long-duration crop, often grown as an intercrop with sorghum or bajra.
Mung bean and urd bean are short-duration crops that fit into the gap between two main crops.
Kharif oilseeds
The main kharif oilseeds are groundnut, soybean, sesame, niger and castor.
Groundnut is grown for its pods, and gypsum applied at pegging improves pod filling.
Soybean needs a well-drained soil and is sensitive to waterlogging.
Castor and niger are hardy crops suited to drier tracts and lighter soils.
Fibre and forage crops
Cotton and jute are the two main fibre crops of the kharif season.
Cotton needs a long frost-free season, and the crop is grown on black soils with good moisture retention.
Forage crops such as forage sorghum, cowpea, cluster bean and maize supply green fodder for livestock.
Perennial grasses such as guinea grass and Napier grass give repeated cuts through the year.
Natural farming: history and importance
Natural farming is an approach that works with natural processes and avoids synthetic inputs.
Indian agriculture has a long heritage of organic and mixed farming that this approach draws on.
Its importance has grown with concern for soil health, water use, climate change and food safety.
It also aims to reduce the cost of cultivation and the dependence on purchased inputs.
Pillars of natural farming
The approach rests on minimal disturbance of the soil, permanent soil cover and diversity of crops.
Mulching with crop residue conserves moisture and feeds the soil organisms.
On-farm preparations and cattle-based inputs are used in place of purchased fertilizer and pesticide.
The design of the farm keeps an ecological balance so that pests are held in check naturally.
Footprints and ecosystem services
An ecological footprint measures the area of land needed to support a given activity.
A water, carbon and nitrogen footprint measures the use or release of each of those in producing a crop.
Ecosystem services are the benefits that nature provides, such as pollination, pest control and nutrient cycling.
Integrating crops, trees and animals on the same farm strengthens these services and spreads risk.
Nutrient management and certification
Nutrients in natural farming come from compost, dung, crop residue, green manure and mineral sources.
Animals are reared on the farm so that dung and urine are available for the preparations.
Certification and standards give the buyer assurance that the produce meets the stated practice.
The economics of natural farming depend on lower input cost, premium price and the yield actually obtained.
Mendel's principles of heredity
Gregor Mendel worked on the garden pea and established the basic laws of inheritance.
The law of segregation states that the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation.
The law of independent assortment states that genes for different traits are inherited independently when they lie on different chromosomes.
A monohybrid cross gives a 3 to 1 ratio in the F2, and a dihybrid cross gives 9 to 3 to 3 to 1.
Chromosome architecture
A chromosome has a centromere, telomeres and, in some cases, a secondary constriction.
The centromere is the point at which the spindle fibres attach during cell division.
Telomeres protect the ends of the chromosome, and chromomeres are the bead-like thickenings along the thread.
The chromosomal theory of inheritance holds that the genes are carried on the chromosomes.
Linkage and chromosome mapping
Linkage is the tendency of genes lying close together on the same chromosome to be inherited together.
Crossing over exchanges segments between homologous chromosomes and breaks the linkage.
The frequency of crossing over between two genes is a measure of the distance between them.
A chromosome map is drawn from these recombination frequencies, with the centiMorgan as the unit of distance.
Mutation
A mutation is a sudden heritable change in the genetic material.
Point mutations change a single base, while chromosomal mutations change the structure or number of chromosomes.
Mutations may be induced by physical agents such as radiation or by chemical mutagens.
Most mutations are harmful, but useful ones are the raw material for breeding new varieties.
Fruit crops: scope and classification
Fruit crops give higher returns per unit area than most field crops and support processing and export.
They are classified as tropical, subtropical and temperate according to the climate they need.
They may also be grouped by their botanical family or by their bearing habit.
India is a leading producer of mango, banana and citrus, though productivity remains below potential.
Planting systems, training and pruning
The planting system decides the arrangement of trees and the use of land and light.
Square, rectangular, quincunx, triangular and hexagonal are the common systems.
Training builds the framework of the young tree, and pruning removes growth that is unwanted or unproductive.
The right canopy lets light into the centre and keeps spraying and harvesting practical.
Tropical and subtropical fruits
Mango is the most important subtropical fruit of India and is propagated by grafting on a rootstock.
Banana is propagated from suckers or tissue-cultured plants, and desuckering keeps the stand clean.
Citrus is propagated by budding, and greening disease is its most serious threat.
Guava, papaya, sapota and pomegranate are the other important crops of this group.
Plantation crops
Coconut, arecanut, oil palm, cashew, cocoa, coffee and tea are the main plantation crops.
Most are perennial and need a long establishment period before they come into bearing.
They are grown on a plantation scale and are important earners of foreign exchange.
Spice crops such as pepper, cardamom and nutmeg are often grown with them as mixed crops.
Plant parasitic nematodes
Nematodes are microscopic, unsegmented roundworms found in soil and water.
Plant parasitic forms have a hollow stylet, which they use to puncture the plant cell and feed.
They live in the soil, in roots, or in the aerial parts of the plant.
Their damage often goes unnoticed because the symptoms appear above ground as poor growth.
Classification and feeding habits
Nematodes are classified up to the family level, with emphasis on genera of economic importance.
They are grouped by feeding habit as ectoparasites, which feed from outside, and endoparasites, which enter the tissue.
Root-knot nematodes of the genus Meloidogyne are the most widely damaging group.
The cyst nematodes and the lesion nematodes are other important genera in field crops.
Symptoms and disease interaction
Above ground, nematode attack shows as stunting, yellowing and poor response to fertilizer.
Below ground, the roots show galls, lesions, forked roots or a stubby, damaged root system.
Nematodes often interact with fungi and bacteria and make the disease far more severe than either alone.
Entomopathogenic nematodes, on the other hand, are useful as biological control agents against insect pests.
Nematode management
Cultural methods include crop rotation with a non-host, fallowing and the use of organic amendments.
Physical methods include soil solarisation and hot water treatment of planting material.
Biological control uses fungi and bacteria that parasitise nematode eggs and juveniles.
Chemical control uses nematicides, and plant resistance combined with these methods gives integrated management.
Soil survey
Soil survey is the systematic examination, description and mapping of the soils of an area.
Its purpose is to classify the soils and to show their extent and distribution on a map.
A detailed survey is used for farm planning, while a reconnaissance survey is used for regional planning.
The soil map is the base document on which all land use decisions rest.
Soil classification and taxonomy
Soil classification groups soils with similar properties so that knowledge can be transferred between them.
The USDA system of soil taxonomy is the most widely used, with orders, suborders, great groups and lower categories.
Diagnostic horizons are the layers that define the classes, such as the surface horizon enriched with organic matter.
Soils of India and Tamil Nadu are mapped under these orders and are used for land use planning.
Land capability classification
Land capability classification groups land by its suitability for cultivation and the risk of damage if used.
It has eight classes: the first four are suited to cultivation, and the last four are not.
The classification considers slope, depth, erosion, drainage and climate.
Irrigability classification and the Storie index are other systems that rate land for a specific use.
Remote sensing, GIS and GPS
Remote sensing records information about the earth's surface from a distance, using sensors.
Energy interaction with the atmosphere and the surface is what the sensor actually measures.
A geographic information system stores and analyses data that has a location.
The global positioning system gives the coordinates of a point, and its data feed into maps and digital elevation models.
Surveying and levelling
Surveying measures the relative positions of points on the earth's surface.
Chain surveying measures distances, and compass surveying measures directions.
Levelling measures the difference in elevation between points using a level and a staff.
Land measurement and levelling are the first steps in planning any soil and water conservation work.
Soil erosion
Soil erosion is the detachment and transport of soil by water, wind or other agents.
Geologic erosion is the slow natural process, while accelerated erosion is caused mainly by human activity.
The universal soil loss equation estimates the average annual soil loss from a slope.
Water erosion passes through the stages of splash, sheet, rill and gully erosion.
Soil conservation and watershed management
Soil conservation is the set of measures that keep the soil in place and maintain its fertility.
Biological measures include contour cultivation, strip cropping and cropping systems that cover the soil.
Mechanical measures include contour bunds, terraces and check dams.
Watershed management treats the whole catchment as a unit, with measures laid out from the ridge to the valley.
Irrigation, drainage, wells and pumps
Flow in an open channel is measured by the velocity-area method or by a weir or notch.
A rectangular weir, a Cippoletti weir and a V notch are the common measuring structures.
Duty of water expresses the area irrigated per unit of water, and it is used in designing a canal.
Wells may be open or tube wells, and the common pumps are reciprocating, centrifugal, turbine, submersible and jet pumps.
